passages.title: The Book and those conscious of Allah who follow it
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat open the longest sūrah of the Qur'an by doing two things at once: the Book announces what it is — a revelation beyond doubt — and it draws a portrait of the people who will actually be guided by it. Ayah 2 makes the claim, ayat 3 and 4 list the qualities, ayah 5 delivers the verdict. Mujahid noticed the architecture: "Four Ayat at the beginning of Surat Al-Baqarah describe the believers, two describe the disbelievers, and thirteen describe the hypocrites." This is the first of those portraits — the one we are meant to recognise ourselves in. Ibn Kathir notes that there is no disagreement that al-Baqarah was revealed in its entirety in Madinah, and that Khalid bin Maʿdan used to call it the *Fusṭāṭ*, the tent, of the Qur'an.

## Alif Lām Mīm: letters we are not meant to crack

Ayah 1 is three Arabic letters pronounced separately, without vowels. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the technical name for such openings: *muqaṭṭaʿāt*, "isolated letters." Ibn Kathir counts them: remove the repetitions and fourteen distinct letters stand at the heads of the sūrahs, and twenty-nine sūrahs begin this way.

What do they mean? Here the honest answer is the scholarly one. Ibn Kathir reports that these letters are "among those things whose knowledge Allah has kept only for Himself" — a view transmitted from Abu Bakr, ʿUmar, ʿUthman, ʿAli and Ibn Masʿud. Others said they are names of the sūrahs, or the beginnings Allah chose to start His sūrahs with; Mujahid held that they are simply letters of the alphabet.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports that while some commentators took the isolated letters as names of the sūrahs and others as symbols of the Divine Names, the majority of the Companions, the *Tābiʿīn* (the generation after them) and the later authoritative scholars preferred the view that these letters are symbols or mysteries whose meaning is known to Allah alone — or that may have been entrusted as a special secret to the Prophet ﷺ, not to be communicated to anyone else. That is why no explanation of them is reported from him. Maʿārif then notes that the great commentator al-Qurtubi adopted this view, and summarises him: according to ʿĀmir al-Shaʿbi, Sufyan al-Thawri and many masters of the science of hadith, every revealed book contains certain secret signs and mysteries of Allah, and these letters belong to the *mutashābihāt* — the verses of hidden meaning, whose sense is known to Allah alone. Al-Qurtubi adds that the Caliphs Abu Bakr, ʿUmar, ʿUthman and ʿAli, and most of the Companions such as Ibn Masʿud, held firmly that these are Allah's secrets: we believe they came down from Allah and recite them exactly as they came down, without being inquisitive about their meanings. Ibn Kathir, citing al-Qurtubi and others, prefers this view as well.

None of that makes them empty. They benefit us still: to believe in them and to recite them is in itself a great merit, and in reciting them we receive spiritual blessings from the unseen world even when we are unaware of it. And Maʿārif is careful to add that interpretations *have* been offered by great and authentic scholars — but their purpose was symbolic, or to awaken readers to the depths of meaning hidden in the Qur'an, never to claim that this is what Allah intended; so such efforts should not be attacked either.

Both commentaries refuse the lazy conclusion. Ibn Kathir is blunt: "There is no doubt that Allah did not reveal these letters for jest and play." To say that some of the Qur'an means nothing is a major mistake. If an authentic narration from the Prophet ﷺ explaining them should be found, we embrace his statement; failing that, we stop where we were made to stop and proclaim, *"We believe in it; all of it is from our Lord"* (3:7). And since the scholars did not settle on one explanation, Ibn Kathir gives a rule of conduct: whoever finds a particular scholar's opinion sound is obliged to follow it, and otherwise it is better to refrain from any judgment on the matter.

One wisdom holds regardless of their meaning: they testify to the miracle of the Qur'an. Allah's servants are unable to produce anything like it **even though it is composed of the very letters they speak to one another with**. Ibn Kathir traces this opinion carefully: ar-Razi mentioned it in his own Tafsir and related it to al-Mubarrid and several other scholars; al-Qurtubi related it to al-Farrāʼ and Qutrub; az-Zamakhshari agreed with it in *al-Kashshāf*; and Ibn Taymiyyah, together with Ibn Kathir's own teacher al-Hafiz al-Mizzi, held it too. Az-Zamakhshari adds a fine observation: the letters were repeated across the sūrahs — one at a time, or two, three, four or five — so that the challenge would be more daring, matching the way words in ordinary speech are built. And Ibn Kathir lines up example after example in which such an opening is followed immediately by a mention of the Book: *Alif Lām Mīm. That is the Book…*, *Alif Lām Mīm Ṣād. A Book sent down to you…*, *Alif Lām Rā. A Book which We have revealed to you…* Here, too, the letters are followed at once by the Book.

## "That Book" — a pointer that reaches backwards

Ayah 2 begins *dhālika al-kitāb*, literally "**that** Book" — and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises this as a genuine grammatical and exegetical problem, since *dhālika* points to something distant, while the Book obviously means the Qur'an, which is present before us. The subtle indication, it says, is that the pronoun refers back to the prayer for the straight path made in Sūrat al-Fātiḥah: the prayer has been granted, and this Book is the answer to the request — the detailed account of that straight path for those who seek guidance and are willing to follow it. The first two sūrahs are one conversation: we ask, and Allah replies, "That is the Book."

**"There is no doubt in it."** *Rayb* means doubt. Ibn Kathir records this explanation from Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn Masʿud and several other Companions, and from Abu ad-Darda', Mujahid, Saʿid bin Jubayr, Qatadah and others; Ibn Abi Hatim said, "I do not know of any disagreement over this explanation." The meaning is that this Book is without doubt revealed from Allah. Some scholars read the phrase as a prohibition: do not doubt the Qur'an. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān meets the obvious objection — that plenty of people *do* doubt it — by distinguishing two sources of doubt: either the statement itself is erroneous and so genuinely open to suspicion, or the listener has misunderstood it, in which case the statement is not really doubtful at all. So in spite of the doubts of a thousand men of small or perverse understanding, it remains true that there is no doubt in this Book, neither in its having been revealed by Allah nor in its contents. Even the recitation pause carries meaning: Ibn Kathir notes that some reciters pause at *lā rayba* and continue *fīhi hudan lil-muttaqīn*, but he prefers pausing after *lā rayba fīhi*, since then "guidance" becomes an attribute of the Qur'an itself — the Book **is** guidance — which carries the better meaning.

## Guidance for the muttaqīn — and why not for everyone

Why guidance for *the God-fearing*, when it is the heedless who seem to need it more? Both commentaries take the question head-on.

First, the word. *Muttaqīn* comes from *taqwā*, whose root meaning Ibn Kathir gives as avoiding what one dislikes; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders it literally "to fear, to refrain from," and in Islamic terminology, fearing Allah and refraining from the transgression of His commandments. The definition that stays with you is a conversation. ʿUmar bin al-Khattab asked Ubayy bin Kaʿb about taqwā. Ubayy said, "Have you ever walked on a path that has thorns on it?" ʿUmar said yes. "What did you do then?" "I rolled up my sleeves and struggled." Ubayy said, "That is taqwā." It is not a mood; it is how you walk.

Ibn ʿAbbas explained the muttaqīn as "the believers who avoid Shirk with Allah and who work in His obedience," and elsewhere as those who fear Allah's punishment — which would follow if they abandoned the guidance they recognise and know — while hoping in His mercy by believing in what He revealed. Qatadah pointed forward: they are the people Allah describes in ayah 3 and the ayat after it. Ibn Jarir held that the ayah includes all of these meanings, and Ibn Kathir calls that the correct view. At-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah narrated that ʿAtiyah as-Saʿdi said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, "The servant will not acquire the status of the Muttaqin until he abandons what is harmless out of fear of falling into that which is harmful." At-Tirmidhi then said, "Hasan Gharib."

Second, the logic. The Qur'an is itself a form of guidance, Ibn Kathir explains, but the guidance in it is only *granted* to the righteous: it is "a guide and a healing" for those who believe, while for those who disbelieve "there is heaviness in their ears" (41:44). He then distinguishes **two kinds of hidāyah**: the faith that resides in the heart, which only Allah can create there (*Verily, you guide not whom you like*, 28:56), and the explaining of the truth, giving direction and leading to it, which is what the Prophet ﷺ did (*And verily, you are indeed guiding to the straight path*, 42:52). One is our work; the other is Allah's gift. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that naming the God-fearing denies guidance to nobody: to those who accept the guidance it holds out the hope of being elevated to that rank, and to those already there it promises further and limitless guidance through this Book.

## The portrait: what the God-fearing actually are

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads ayat 3 and 4 as a deliberate delineation: these are the people who have received guidance, whose path is the straight path, and whoever seeks that path should join their company, adopt their beliefs and their way of life. It also shows how much is compressed into ayah 3. Faith is the most important of the three qualities, since it is the basic principle of all other principles and no good deed is valid or accepted without it. The remaining obligations pertain either to a person's own body or to his possessions — so *ṣalāh* is named as the foremost of bodily worship and *infāq*, spending, covers every form of worship involving wealth. Three phrases, and Islam is inside them.

**"Who believe in the unseen."** On *īmān*, Ibn Kathir gathers the early views: Ibn Masʿud said "Iman is to trust," and Ibn ʿAbbas that it means they trust; az-Zuhri said, "Iman is the deeds"; ar-Rabiʿ bin Anas said it means they fear Allah. Ibn Jarir at-Tabari preferred that they be described as having faith "by the tongue, deed and creed" — a general term that includes affirming and believing in Allah, His Books and His Messengers, and then realising that affirmation by living up to what the tongue has uttered. And Ibn Kathir states the Sunni position plainly: when *īmān* is used without restriction it includes beliefs, deeds and statements of the tongue — and **īmān increases and decreases**.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sharpens the word further. Lexically, *īmān* means accepting someone's statement with complete certitude out of total confidence and trust in him. Endorsing what you can observe for yourself is therefore not *īmān*: if one man calls a piece of cloth black and another agrees, that is *taṣdīq* (confirmation), because it rests on personal observation and involves no trust in the speaker. In the language of the Sharīʿah, *īmān* is accepting with complete certitude what a prophet has said, out of total confidence in him and without needing to see it yourself. So faith is not mere information: Satan himself possesses a mental knowledge of the truth, and many disbelievers knew very well that the Prophet ﷺ was truthful and his teaching true, yet did not accept it in their hearts.

*Al-Ghayb*, lexically, denotes things not known to man in an evident manner and not apprehensible through the five senses. Abu al-ʿĀliyah's explanation, which Qatadah echoed, is: "They believe in Allah, His angels, Books, Messengers, the Last Day, His Paradise, Fire and in the meeting with Him… All of this is the Ghayb." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān includes the essence and attributes of Allah, matters pertaining to destiny, Heaven and Hell and what they contain, the Day of Judgment, the Divine Books and the earlier prophets — everything, in short, that the Prophet ﷺ has taught us, on the necessary condition that the teaching reached us through authentic and undeniable sources.

There is honour in believing this way. Ibn Masʿud, when his companions remarked that the Companions' deeds surpassed their own, replied: "The matter of Muhammad ﷺ was clear for those who saw him. By He other than Whom there is no God, no person will ever acquire a better type of faith than believing in Al-Ghayb" — and then recited these very ayat through to "the successful." Ahmad recorded from Abu Jumuʿah that when Abu ʿUbaydah asked whether any people were better than they, who had embraced Islam with the Prophet ﷺ and fought alongside him, he answered: "Yes, those who will come after you, who will believe in me although they did not see me." That is a description of whoever reads these lines.

**"And establish the prayer."** The verb is not "they pray" but *yuqīmūn*, from *iqāmah* — signifying "to straighten out," as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains. It implies not merely saying one's prayers but performing them correctly in every possible way and observing all the prescribed conditions, whether obligatory (*farḍ*), necessary (*wājib*) or commendable (*mustaḥabb*), with regularity and perpetuity, and with inward concentration, humility and awe. Ibn ʿAbbas said it means performing the prayer with all of the obligations that accompany it — completing the bowings, prostrations, recitation, humbleness and attendance for the prayer.

**"And spend out of what We have provided them."** Ibn ʿAbbas is reported as explaining this as the zakāh due on wealth, and in another report as a man's spending on his family, from before zakāh was made obligatory. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the position adopted by the majority of commentators: it includes every form of spending in Allah's way, the obligatory zakāh, necessary alms and voluntary charity alike. Two small words then do enormous work. *Mimmā razaqnāhum*, "out of what **We** have provided them," draws our attention to the fact that anything and everything we possess is a gift from Allah and His trust in our hands — so that even spending all of it would be no favour to Him. And *min* means "part of": in His mercy He asks for a portion, not the whole. Ibn Kathir notes why prayer and spending are paired so often: prayer is a right of Allah and a form of worshipping Him, involving devotion, praise, glorification, supplication and the display of one's dependence on Him, while spending is kindness towards creatures — and those most deserving of it are one's relatives, wife, servants, and then the rest of the people.

**"And who believe in what has been revealed to you and what was revealed before you."** Ibn ʿAbbas explained this as believing in what Allah sent the Prophet ﷺ with and in what the previous Messengers were sent with: "they do not distinguish between them, nor do they reject what they brought from their Lord." Ibn Kathir stresses that these four opening ayat are general and include every believer — Arab, non-Arab, or a person of a previous Scripture, jinn or human — and that the qualities require one another: it is not possible to believe in the unseen, pray and give zakāh while refusing to believe in what the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and the Messengers before him were sent with.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports from the Companions Ibn Masʿud and Ibn ʿAbbas that in the days of the Prophet ﷺ the God-fearing were of two kinds: those who had been associators and disbelievers and then accepted Islam, and those who had been among the People of the Book and embraced Islam later. Ayah 3 refers to the first group, ayah 4 to the second — hence its specific mention of the earlier Divine Books, since according to the hadith this second group deserves a double recompense: for believing in and following the earlier Books before the Qur'an came to replace them, and for believing in and following the Qur'an when it came. Ibn Kathir mentions the same double reward, then balances it: the faith of many Arabs in Islam may be more complete and firmer, so other Muslims of firmer faith might gain a reward equal to those two — "and Allah knows best."

What does that belief mean today? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is precise: everything Allah revealed in the earlier Books is true, excepting the changes and distortions introduced into them, and it was incumbent on the peoples they were sent to that they act by them — but now that all the earlier Books and Sharīʿahs have been abrogated, one must act by the Qur'an alone. In line with this, the Prophet ﷺ taught that when the People of the Book narrate something, neither reject nor affirm what they say, but say: "We believe in what was revealed to us and what was revealed to you." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also reads the very wording of the ayah as an argument for the finality of prophethood: wherever the Qur'an defines faith it speaks of what was revealed **before you** — always *min qabl*, in some forty or fifty places, and nowhere *min baʿd*, never a Book or Prophet still to come. Had revelation been meant to continue, this was precisely the place to say so.

**"And in the Hereafter they are certain."** Ibn Kathir spells out what this includes: the resurrection, the standing on the Day of Resurrection, Paradise, the Fire, the reckoning, and the Scale on which deeds are weighed. *Al-Ākhirah* is so named, he says, because it comes after this earthly life. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that lexically it signifies "that which comes after something," and in this context stands in contrast to the physical world — the other world, beyond physical reality and beyond what our senses or reason can reach. Though faith in it already sits inside faith in the unseen, it is singled out because it may be regarded as the most important constituent of faith in this respect: it is what inspires a person to translate faith into practice. Along with the Oneness of Allah and prophethood, it is the third doctrine common to all the prophets, on which all the Sharīʿahs agree.

Now catch the verb. Of the Hereafter the ayah does not say *yu'minūn* (they believe) but *yūqinūn* — **they have complete certitude**. The opposite of belief is denial; the opposite of certitude is doubt and hesitation. So perfection of faith here is not oral affirmation but a certainty leaving no room for doubt — the kind that comes when one has seen a thing with one's own eyes, with the whole scene of judgment held constantly before them. A man who amasses wealth by usurping what rightfully belongs to others may declare his faith in the Hereafter a thousand times, and the Sharīʿah will still deal with him as a Muslim in worldly concerns, but he does not possess the certitude the Qur'an demands. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out why this reaches where no human law can: penal laws restrain a man only as far as he fears being caught, but the God-fearing man knows for certain that even in the secrecy of a sealed room and in the darkness of night somebody is watching him, and somebody is writing down the smallest thing he does.

## The verdict: on guidance from their Lord, and successful

Ayah 5 is the verdict, and its force lies in the repeated demonstrative *ulā'ika* — "**those** are the ones," said twice. Ibn Kathir explains that "they" gathers up everyone just described: those who believe in the Unseen, establish the prayer, spend from what Allah has granted them, believe in what Allah revealed to the Messenger and to the Messengers before him, and believe in the Hereafter with certainty — and he adds one thing more about them: they prepare the necessary requirements for the Hereafter by performing good deeds and avoiding the prohibitions. *ʿAlā hudan min rabbihim*, "on guidance from their Lord": they are following a light and guidance, he says, and have insight from Allah. *Al-muflihūn*, "the successful," he explains as success in this world and the Hereafter — they shall have what they seek and be saved from the evil they tried to avoid, so that theirs will be reward, eternal life in Paradise, and safety from the torment Allah has prepared for His enemies. And Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads the whole passage as an invitation: this is the guidance and triumph that certitude brings in its wake, and whoever seeks the straight path should join their company.

## Living it

- **Keep this sūrah alive in your home.** In Musnad Ahmad, Sahih Muslim, at-Tirmidhi and an-Nasa'i, Abu Hurayrah reported that the Prophet ﷺ said, "Do not turn your houses into graves. Verily, Shaytan does not enter the house where Surat Al-Baqarah is recited." At-Tirmidhi said, "Hasan Sahih." In his Musnad, ad-Darimi records that Ibn Masʿud said: whoever recites ten ayat of al-Baqarah in a night — the four from the beginning, Ayat al-Kursi (255), the two following it (256–257) and the last three — Shaytan will not enter his house that night.
- **Carry it; don't just store it.** At-Tirmidhi, an-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah recorded from Abu Hurayrah that the Prophet ﷺ compared one who learns the Qur'an, recites it and adheres to it to "a bag that is full of musk whose scent fills the air," and one who learns it and then sleeps while it is in his memory to "a bag that has musk, but is closed tight." This is at-Tirmidhi's wording, and he said the hadith is Hasan.
- **Walk the thorny path.** Ubayy's answer to ʿUmar is ayah 2's ethic in one image: you gather your clothes and pick your steps.

Ayah 2 puts a hard question to anyone who has read the Qur'an and felt nothing: the guidance is there, beyond doubt — so what stands between me and it? These ayat answer that the Book is guidance in itself, but its guidance is granted to those who come to it with taqwā. The difference, then, lies in the reader. Believe what you cannot see because you trust the One who told you; straighten your prayer; open your hand; be certain of the Day you will stand.

# Those Who Persist in Disbelief (2:6–7)

These two ayat turn from the believers described in the opening verses to a very different group: people who, as the commentators describe them, recognise the truth and refuse it anyway. Ayah 6 states the outcome — warning them changes nothing. Ayah 7 gives the reason — their hearts, hearing and sight have been closed.

## Where these ayat sit in the Surah

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lays out the architecture. After affirming that this Book is guidance beyond doubt, the first five ayat describe those who take full benefit from it — named **Muʼminūn** (true believers) or **Muttaqūn** (the God-fearing) — and set out the qualities that distinguish them from others. The next fifteen ayat describe those who refuse that guidance and even oppose it out of spite.

In the Prophet's ﷺ time these fell into two groups. Some came out in open hostility and rejection: the Qurʼān calls them **kāfirūn**, disbelievers. Others, out of moral depravity and greed, lacked even the courage to speak their minds and express their disbelief clearly, and took instead the way of deceit and duplicity. They tried to convince the Muslims that they had faith in the Qurʼān and its teachings and would stand with them against the disbelievers, while nursing denial and rejection in their hearts and assuring the disbelievers privately that they had nothing to do with Islam and mixed with the Muslims only to deceive and spy on them. These the Qurʼān calls **munāfiqūn**, hypocrites.

So of those fifteen ayat, the first two — our passage — deal with the open disbelievers, and the remaining thirteen with the hypocrites, their signs and characteristics and their ultimate end. Ibn Kathir notes the same sequence: four ayat at the beginning of the Surah described the believers, these two describe the disbelievers, and afterwards Allah begins to describe the hypocrites, who show belief and hide disbelief. Because their matter is vague and many people do not realise their true reality, Allah described them in detail — and each characteristic mentioned is itself a type of hypocrisy. Allah revealed Sūrat Barāʼah (9) and Sūrat al-Munāfiqūn (63) about them, and mentioned them in Sūrat an-Nūr (24) and other Surahs, so that their description would be known and their ways and errors avoided.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the larger picture: taking the first twenty ayat together, the Qurʼān points on the one hand to the source of guidance — the Book itself — and on the other divides mankind into two distinct groups on the basis of accepting or rejecting that guidance. The first are those whose path is the object of the prayer at the end of al-Fātiḥah, *"the path of those on whom You have bestowed Your grace"*; the second are those against whose path refuge has been sought, *"not of those who have incurred Your wrath, nor of those who have gone astray."*

And note what the dividing line is not. A division of mankind into groups must, in order to be meaningful, rest on differences of **principle**, not on considerations of birth, race, colour, geography or language. The Qurʼān's clear verdict in this respect: *"It was He that created you: yet some of you are disbelievers and some of you are believers"* (64:2).

## The word *kufr*: covering something over

Ibn Kathir glosses *alladhīna kafarū* — "those who disbelieve" — as those who **covered the truth and hid it**.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the root. Lexically the word means to hide, to conceal. Ingratitude is also called *kufr*, because it involves concealing or covering up a kindness someone has shown.

In the terminology of the Sharīʿah, *kufr* signifies the denial of any of those things in which it is obligatory to believe. The quintessence of *īmān*, and the very basis of the Islamic creed, is that one should confirm with the heart and believe with certitude everything the Prophet ﷺ brought down to us from Allah and which has been established by definite and conclusive proof; so a man who has the temerity to question or disregard even a single teaching of this kind is described as a *kāfir*.

## *Indhār*: a warning that comes from love

The word translated "warn" in ayah 6 is *indhār*, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens it beautifully. *Indhār* signifies bringing news that should cause alarm or concern; its opposite, *ibshār*, signifies bringing good news that should make people rejoice.

But *indhār* is not the ordinary kind of warning meant simply to frighten people. It is one **motivated by compassion and love** — just as one warns one's children against fire, or snakes, or beasts. Hence a thief or a bandit or an aggressor who warns or threatens others cannot be called a *nadhīr*, a warner. That title is specially reserved for the prophets (ʿalayhim as-salām), for they warn people against the pains and punishments of the other world out of compassion and love for their fellow men.

In choosing this title for the prophets, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes, the Qurʼān has made the subtle suggestion that for those who go out to reform others it is not enough merely to convey a message: they must speak to their listeners **with sympathy, understanding and a genuine regard for their good**.

## Why the warning does not land

Ibn Kathir: since Allah had written that these people would cover the truth, it does not matter whether the Prophet ﷺ warns them or not — they would still have disbelieved in what he was sent with. He brings parallel ayat: *"Truly, those against whom the Word of your Lord has been justified, will not believe. Even if every sign should come to them, until they see the painful torment"* (10:96–97); and of the rebellious People of the Book, *"even if you were to bring to the People of the Book all the Ayat, they would not follow your Qiblah"* (2:145).

These ayat, Ibn Kathir says, indicate that whomever Allah has written to be miserable shall never find anyone to guide him to happiness, and whomever Allah directs to misguidance shall never find anyone to guide him. So — do not pity them, O Muhammad ﷺ; deliver the Message to them. Whoever among them accepts it shall gain the best rewards; as for those who turn away in rejection, do not feel sad for them or concerned about them, for *"Your duty is only to convey the Message and on Us is the reckoning"* (13:40), and *"But you are only a warner. And Allah is a Wakīl — Disposer of affairs, Trustee, Guardian — over all things"* (11:12).

ʿAlī bin Abī Ṭalḥah reported that Ibn ʿAbbās said about this ayah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ **was eager for all the people to believe** and to follow the guidance he was sent with; Allah informed him that none would believe except those for whom He decreed happiness in the first place, and none would stray except those whom Allah had decreed to do so in the first place.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that this comes as a **comfort** to the Prophet ﷺ: some of the disbelievers are so vain, arrogant and opinionated that, in spite of recognising the truth, they stubbornly persist in their refusal and are not prepared to hear the truth or to see obvious proofs — so all the efforts he makes to reform and convert them will bear no fruit, and for them it is all one whether he tries or not.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also notes the usual way of Allah with such depraved people: they are given a certain kind of punishment even in this world — their hearts are sealed and their eyes and ears stopped against the truth, so that as far as truth is concerned they become as if they have no mind to think, no eyes to see and no ears to listen. The last phrase of ayah 7 speaks of the grievous punishment reserved for them in the other world.

## Two precisions that prevent a serious misreading

**First — who "they will not believe" refers to.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is explicit: the prediction *lā yuʼminūn*, "they shall not believe," is specifically related to those disbelievers who refused to listen to the Prophet ﷺ and who, as Allah knew, were going to die as disbelievers. **This does not apply to disbelievers in general**, for there were many who later accepted Islam.

**Second — the word *ʿalayhim*, "for them."** In announcing that it is all one whether the Prophet ﷺ warns them or not, the Qurʼān adds the qualification *ʿalayhim* — "for them." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out that this clearly indicates it is all one for the disbelievers alone, and not for the Prophet ﷺ, for he would in any case get a reward for bringing the message of Allah to his fellow men and for his efforts to teach and reform them. That is why there is not a single ayah in the Qurʼān which would dissuade him from calling even such people to Islam. From this we may infer: **the man who strives to spread the Word of Allah and to reform his fellow men always gets a reward for his good deed, even if he has not been effective.**

## Ayah 7: the seal and the covering

Ayah 7 explains the reason. As Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it: Allah has set a seal on their hearts and ears, there is a covering on their eyes, all the avenues of knowing and understanding are thus closed, and it would be futile to expect any change in them. A thing is sealed so that nothing may enter it from outside; the setting of a seal on their hearts and ears also means that they have altogether lost the capacity for accepting the truth.

**Why a seal there, and a covering on the eyes?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān (citing Mazharī) draws the subtle distinction: an idea can enter the heart from all possible directions and not from one direction alone, and so can a sound enter the ears — such openings can be blocked only by sealing them. The eyes, on the contrary, work in one direction only and can see only what lies in front of them; if there is a covering on them, they cease to function.

Ibn Kathir makes a parallel observation about recitation: reciting "Allah has set a seal on their hearts and on their hearing," then pausing, then continuing with "and on their eyes there is a *ghishāwah* (covering)," is accurate, for the stamp is placed on the heart and the hearing while the covering is appropriately placed on the eyes. In his Tafsir, As-Suddi said that Ibn ʿAbbās and Ibn Masʿūd said about "Allah has set a seal on their hearts and on their hearing": "So that they neither understand nor hear" — and that Allah placed a covering on their sight, meaning their eyes, and so they do not see.

**What *khatama* means.** As-Suddi said *khatama Allāh* means "Allah has sealed." Qatādah said the ayah means: Shayṭān controlled them when they obeyed him, therefore Allah sealed their hearts, hearing and sight, and they could neither see the guidance nor hear, comprehend or understand it. Ibn Jurayj said that Mujāhid said of "Allah has set a seal on their hearts": "A stamp. It occurs when sin resides in the heart and surrounds it from all sides, and this submersion of the heart in sin constitutes a stamp, meaning a seal." Ibn Jurayj also said that the seal is placed on the heart and the hearing. And Ibn Jurayj said that ʿAbdullāh bin Kathīr narrated that Mujāhid said: **"The stain is not as bad as the stamp, the stamp is not as bad as the lock, which is the worst type."**

Al-Aʿmash preserved the image: "Mujāhid demonstrated with his hand while saying, 'They used to say that the heart is just like this' — meaning the open palm. When the servant commits a sin, a part of the heart will be rolled up — and he rolled up his index finger. When the servant commits another sin, another part of the heart will be rolled up — and he rolled up another finger, until he had rolled up all his fingers. Then he said: **'Then, the heart will be sealed.'**" Mujāhid also said that this is the description of the *rān*, the stain, referred to in 83:14.

Al-Qurṭubī said: the Ummah has agreed that Allah has described Himself with sealing and closing the hearts of the disbelievers **as a punishment for their disbelief** — as in *"Nay, Allah has set a seal upon their hearts because of their disbelief"* (4:155).

## From the Sunnah

Al-Qurṭubī then mentioned the hadith about the changing of hearts, in which the Prophet ﷺ supplicated: **"O You Who changes the hearts, make our hearts firm on Your religion."**

He also mentioned the hadith of Ḥudhayfah recorded in the Ṣaḥīḥ, in which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that the *fitan* — trials and tests — are offered to the hearts, just as the straws that are sewn into a woven mat, one after another. Any heart that accepts them has a black dot engraved on it; any heart that rejects them has a white dot engraved on it. The hearts therefore become two categories: one white, just like the barren rock, which no *fitnah* shall ever harm as long as the heavens and earth still exist; and another black, just as a cup turned upside down, a heart that does not recognise righteousness or renounce evil.

Ibn Jarīr said: the truth regarding this subject is what the authentic hadith from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ stated. Abū Hurayrah narrated that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that when the believer commits a sin, a black dot is engraved on his heart; if he repents, refrains and regrets, his heart is polished again; but if he commits more errors, the dots increase until they cover his heart — and that is the *rān* Allah described: *"Nay! But on their hearts is the Ran (stain) which they used to earn"* (83:14). At-Tirmidhī, an-Nasāʼī and Ibn Mājah recorded this hadith, and at-Tirmidhī said it is *ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ*.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān recounts the same teaching from a hadith, adding the picture of that first dot disturbing a man the way a smudge on a white cloth is always displeasing to us; but if, instead of asking Allah's pardon for the first sin, he proceeds to a second, another dot shows up, and with every new sin the black dots go on multiplying till the whole heart turns dark, and he can no longer see good as good nor evil as evil, and grows quite incapable of making such distinctions — the darkness the Qurʼān calls *rān*, rust. It also cites another authentic hadith reported by Tirmidhī from the Companion Abū Hurayrah ؓ, that the Prophet ﷺ said: "When a man commits a sin, his heart grows dark, **but if he seeks Allah's pardon, it becomes clear again.**"

## Losing the favour is itself the punishment

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the practical lesson. These two ayat tell us that the other world is the place where one receives the real punishment for disbelief or for some of one's sins — ayah 7 ends with *"theirs will be a great torment."* One may, however, receive some punishment for certain sins even in this world; and such a punishment sometimes takes a very grievous form — the divine favour that helps a person to reform himself is **withdrawn**, so that, ignoring how his deeds are to be assessed on the Day of Judgment, he keeps growing in disobedience and sin, and finally comes to lose even the awareness of evil. In delineating such a situation, certain elders have remarked that *one punishment for an evil deed is another evil deed which comes after, and one reward for a good deed is another good deed which comes after.*

## "Then how can they be blamed?"

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān answers the objection head-on. If Allah Himself has sealed their hearts and blocked their senses, are they not helpless — unable to be held responsible for what they did not choose, and so undeserving of punishment?

Put ayah 7 beside 83:14, *"No. But what they did has rusted their hearts."* That ayah makes it plain that it is **their own arrogance and their own evil deeds** that have settled on their hearts as rust; and in the ayah under discussion it is this very rust that is described as a seal and a covering. Considering the two ayat together, we can easily see why they should be punished: in adopting the way of arrogance and pride they have, wilfully and out of their own choice, destroyed their capacity for accepting the truth, and thus are themselves the authors of their own ruin. But Allah, being the Creator of all the actions of His creatures, has in ayah 7 attributed to Himself the setting of the seal on their hearts and ears, thus pointing out that when these people insisted, as a matter of their own choice, on destroying their aptitude for receiving the truth, Allah produced — as is His way in such cases — the state of insensitivity in their hearts and senses.

**What the passage asks of us.** Three things follow from what the commentators have said. Guard the heart while it is still soft: on the hadith Ibn Jarīr cites, every sin engraves a black dot, and repenting, desisting and regretting polishes the heart again — and as the report from Abū Hurayrah has it, when a man's heart grows dark through sin, seeking Allah's pardon makes it clear again. Second, be careful whom you count as beyond reach: Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states that "they shall not believe" was said specifically of those disbelievers who refused to listen and were going to die in disbelief, and does not apply to disbelievers in general, for there were many who later accepted Islam. And third, carry the message the way a *nadhīr* carries it — with the compassion of someone warning a child away from fire, speaking with sympathy, understanding and genuine regard for the listener's good — knowing that the one who strives to spread the Word of Allah always gets his reward, even if he has not been effective, because *"Your duty is only to convey the Message and on Us is the reckoning."*

passages.title: The hypocrites' hollow claim to belief
passages.tafsir:
These nine ayat draw a portrait of a third kind of person. Sūrah al-Baqarah opens by declaring the Book to be beyond doubt, and then, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lays out the structure, sorts humanity by their response to it: the first five ayat describe *al-muttaqūn*, the Allah-fearing; the next two describe *al-kāfirūn*, those whose rejection was open and violent; and the following thirteen — beginning here at ayah 8 — describe *al-munāfiqūn*, the hypocrites: those crafty disbelievers who claimed to be Muslims and in reality were not.

What holds ayat 8–16 together is a single sustained exposure. The passage is built as an argument: they speak, and Allah answers; they speak again, and Allah answers again — four claims, four verdicts — and the whole exchange is finally priced as a business deal that lost everything. Underneath the speaking is a diagnosis (a disease in the heart), and running through the answers is one refrain: *they do not perceive it, they do not know*.

## What hypocrisy is

Ibn Kathir defines *nifāq* as showing conformity — or agreement — while concealing evil. He distinguishes types: hypocrisy in creed, whose people reside in the Fire for eternity, and hypocrisy in deed, which is one of the major sins. Ibn Jurayj described the hypocrite memorably: "His actual deeds are different from what he publicizes, what he conceals is different from what he utters, his entrance and presence are not the same as his exit and absence."

Qatadah's description, reported by Saʿīd, is worth sitting with. The hypocrite "is devious, he says the truth with his tongue and defies it with his heart and deeds. He wakes up in a condition other than the one he goes to sleep in, and goes to sleep in a different condition than the one he wakes up in. He changes his mind just like a ship that moves about whenever a wind blows." That is the governing image of the whole passage — not a villain with a plan, but a man with no fixed keel.

## Where these people came from

Ibn Kathir gives the history that unlocks the passage. The revelations describing the characteristics of the hypocrites came down in Madinah, because there were no hypocrites in Makkah at all. There the situation ran the opposite way: some people were forced to pretend that they were disbelievers while their hearts concealed their faith.

After the Prophet ﷺ migrated to Madinah, he found the Anṣār of Aws and Khazraj, who had worshipped idols in the pre-Islamic period of ignorance, and three Jewish tribes: Banū Qaynuqāʿ, allies of Khazraj, and Banū an-Naḍīr and Banū Qurayẓah, allies of Aws. Many members of Aws and Khazraj embraced Islam; only a few Jews did, such as ʿAbdullāh bin Salām. In that early Madinan stage there were still no hypocrites, because the Muslims were not strong enough to be feared yet, and the Prophet ﷺ had concluded peace treaties with the Jews and with several other Arab tribes around Madinah.

Then came Badr, and Allah gave victory to Islam and its people. Ibn Kathir singles out one man: ʿAbdullāh bin Ubayy bin Salūl, chief of Khazraj and, during Jāhiliyyah, master of both tribes — they were about to appoint him their king when the Message reached Madinah and many there embraced Islam. His heart filled with hatred against Islam and its people. When Badr took place he said, "Allah's religion has become apparent" — and so he pretended to be Muslim, along with many who were just like him, as well as many among the People of the Book. It was then, says Ibn Kathir, that hypocrisy began in Madinah and among the surrounding nomad tribes. And he adds a striking exception: none of the Emigrants were hypocrites, since they emigrated willingly, seeking the pleasure of Allah — a man who emigrated from Makkah was forced to abandon all his wealth, offspring and land, and no one pays that price for a pretence.

Who exactly is addressed here? Muhammad bin Isḥāq narrated that Ibn ʿAbbās said ayah 8 refers to "the hypocrites among the Aws and Khazraj and those who behaved as they did," and Ibn Kathir notes that Abū al-ʿĀliyah, al-Ḥasan, Qatadah and as-Suddī explained the ayah the same way. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is more specific: it says that to grasp these ayat fully one should bear in mind that the hypocrites in question were actually Jews — people for whom belief in Allah and in the Hereafter was already part of their creed, while belief in the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ was not. Ibn Kathir's own historical account, which mentions "many among the People of the Book" pretending Islam after Badr, sits alongside this.

Why expose them at all? Ibn Kathir answers plainly: Allah revealed the characteristics of the hypocrites so that the believers would not be deceived by their outer appearance, thus saving the believers from a great evil — for to consider sinners as righteous people is extremely dangerous.

## Could they be told apart?

This question runs across the passage, and the sources handle it with care.

Ibn Kathir notes that the scholars who held that the Prophet ﷺ knew the hypocrites of his time have as evidence only the hadith of Ḥudhayfah bin al-Yamān, in which the Prophet ﷺ gave him the names of fourteen hypocrites during the battle of Tabūk — men who plotted to kill him at night on a hill by exciting his camel so that she would throw him down, a plot which Allah disclosed to him. But of the others Allah said, of the bedouins around Madinah and some of its people who persist in hypocrisy, *"you know them not, We know them"* (9:101); and *"Had We willed, We could have shown them to you, and you should have known them by their marks; but surely, you will know them by the tone of their speech"* (47:30). These ayat prove, says Ibn Kathir, that the Prophet ﷺ was not informed about each and every one of the hypocrites of his time; he was informed of their characteristics, and used to assume that certain people possessed them.

The most notorious of them was Ibn Ubayy, to whom the Companion Zayd bin Arqam gave truthful testimony. When ʿUmar bin al-Khaṭṭāb once mentioned Ibn Ubayy's case to the Prophet ﷺ, he said, "I would not like the Arabs to say to each other that Muhammad ﷺ is killing his Companions." And when Ibn Ubayy died, the Prophet ﷺ performed the funeral prayer for him and attended his funeral just as he used to do with other Muslims; it was recorded in the Ṣaḥīḥ that he said, "I was given the choice, so I chose," and in another narration, "If I knew that by asking Allah to forgive him more than seventy times He would forgive him, then I would do that."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān carries the question past the Prophet's ﷺ lifetime. In his time a hypocrite could be identified in one of two ways: Allah informed him through revelation, or a man showed himself up by some word or deed overtly repugnant to the Islamic creed or practice. Revelation ceased with the Prophet's ﷺ departure from this world, so the first route is no longer available; the second remains. Al-ʿAynī, in his commentary on al-Bukhārī, reports from Imam Mālik that after the days of the Prophet ﷺ this is the only available means of identifying hypocrisy. And since the disbelief of such a man is then proven by clear and definite evidence, the Sharīʿah does not place him in a separate category but deals with him as it would deal with any other *kāfir*.

The same source uses this passage to define a phrase often misunderstood — that the *Ahl al-Qiblah*, those who turn towards the Kaʿbah in prayer, cannot be branded infidels. The term pertains only to those who do not deny any of the basic essential doctrines and commandments of Islam, the *ḍarūriyyāt*. Even the hypocrites of the Qurʼān offered their prayers exactly as the Muslims did, and facing the Kaʿbah was not taken to be sufficient to make them acceptable as true Muslims, simply because they did not have faith in all the essentials as the Companions did.

## The disease under the words

Before any of their sentences are answered, ayah 10 names what is producing them: *fī qulūbihim maraḍ* — "in their hearts is a disease."

As-Suddī narrated from Abū Mālik and from Abū Ṣāliḥ, from Ibn ʿAbbās, and Murrah al-Hamdānī from Ibn Masʿūd and other Companions, that the disease here means **doubt**, and that the increase is likewise doubt. Mujāhid, ʿIkrimah, al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, Abū al-ʿĀliyah, ar-Rabīʿ bin Anas and Qatadah said similarly. ʿAbdur-Raḥmān bin Zayd bin Aslam specified: "A disease in the religion, not a physical disease. They are the hypocrites and the disease is the doubt that they brought to Islam" — and the increase, he said, is an increase in shameful behaviour, reciting 9:124–125, where revelation increases the believers in faith and joy but "will add disgrace to their disgrace" for those in whose hearts is a disease: "evil to their evil and deviation to their deviation." Ibn Kathir affirms this and names the principle — a punishment compatible to the sin, as the earlier scholars stated. The mirror image is 47:17: *"as for those who accept guidance, He increases their guidance and grants them their piety."*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān develops the metaphor. Disease in the general medical sense is a state in which a man has lost the balanced proportion of the elements that keep him healthy, so that his body can no longer function properly, which may finally lead to his total destruction. The Qurʼān and the Hadith apply the word also to states of the soul which gradually deprive a man of the ability to perform good deeds, and even of ordinary human decency, till he meets his spiritual death. Junaid of Baghdad said that just as the diseases of the body arise from an imbalance among the four humours, the diseases of the heart arise from a surrender to one's physical desires. In the hypocrite's case the illness is bodily too, since he is always shuddering for fear of being exposed; and jealousy being a necessary ingredient of hypocrisy, he cannot bear to see the Muslims growing stronger, yet cannot even unburden his heart of the venom. It is Allah's will to make the position of the Muslims stronger still — which is precisely what keeps feeding the malady.

Then comes the reason for the punishment: *"because they used to tell lies."* Ibn Kathir notes that the hypocrites have two characteristics — they lie, and they deny the Unseen. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān flags something subtle here. Their greatest crime was disbelief and hypocrisy in matters of faith, and they were committing other crimes too, nursing envy and malice and actually conspiring against the Muslims — and yet the grievous punishment is connected to their habit of telling lies. The indication is that this nefarious habit was basically their real crime, the one that gradually led them to hypocrisy and disbelief. That is why the Qurʼān joins lying to idol worship in a single phrase: *"Guard yourselves against the filth of idols and against telling lies"* (22:30).

## Four claims, four verdicts

**"We believe in Allah and the Last Day."** Read their sentence closely, and notice what is missing. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out that in claiming to be Muslims they mentioned only faith in Allah and in the Day of Judgment, leaving out faith in the Prophet ﷺ — for fear of telling a lie. And it draws the moral: see how disgusting lying is, that even these men, with all their hostility to Islam, tried to refrain from it as far as they could.

Allah's answer is *wa mā hum bi-muʼminīn*, "they are not believers." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains why the careful formula still fails. To be a Muslim it is not enough to declare faith in Allah and the Hereafter in whatever form or manner suits one's fancy — associators of every kind believe in Allah in some way and consider Him Omnipotent, and the Qurʼān does not let any of that pass for faith. Faith in Allah must conform to what the Qurʼān specifically lays down regarding the divine names and attributes; belief in the Hereafter is valid only when it is true to the specifications of the Qurʼān and the Hadith. By that measure their claim failed on both counts: they regarded the Prophet ʿUzair (Ezra) as a son of Allah, and cherished the belief that the progeny of the prophets, however they acted, would always remain chosen and would not be called to account.

Ibn Kathir sets ayah 8 beside 63:1 — *"When the hypocrites come to you, they say: 'We bear witness that you are indeed the Messenger of Allah'"* — words uttered only when they meet you, with their tongues alone; and the same ayah delivers the verdict, *"And Allah bears witness that the hypocrites are indeed liars."*

Ayah 9 presses the same claim further: *"They try to deceive Allah and those who believe."* Ibn Kathir says they show belief outwardly while concealing disbelief, thinking that this will mislead Allah, or that the statements they utter will help them with Allah — and this, he says, is an indication of their total ignorance. Compare 58:18: on the Day Allah resurrects them all together they will swear to Him as they swear to you, thinking they have something to stand upon. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that probably none of them could even have entertained such a delusion as deceiving Allah; what they were actually doing was trying to deceive the Prophet ﷺ and the Muslims. Allah equates the two — and the indication is that a man who is in any way impertinent to a prophet or a man of Allah is ultimately impertinent to Allah Himself, above all in the case of the Prophet ﷺ. The attempt is futile in both directions: Allah cannot possibly be deceived, and divine revelation protects the Prophet ﷺ from all trickery. Hence: *"they only deceive themselves, and they do not perceive it."*

**"We are only peacemakers."** Told not to make mischief on the earth, they answered with a claim of pure good will. In as-Suddī's Tafsir, Ibn ʿAbbās and Ibn Masʿūd said the corruption forbidden here is "disbelief and acts of disobedience." Abū al-ʿĀliyah, reported through ar-Rabīʿ bin Anas, said whoever disobeys Allah on the earth, or commands that Allah be disobeyed, has committed mischief on it — "peace on both the earth and in the heavens is ensured through obedience to Allah."

Ibn Jarīr catalogues their mischief: disobeying their Lord and continuing in the prohibited acts, abandoning what Allah made obligatory, doubting His religion, lying to the believers by saying the contrary of the doubt and hesitation their hearts harbour, and giving as much aid as they can against Allah's loyal friends while supporting those who deny Allah, His Books and His Messengers — "while thinking that they are doing righteous work on earth." Ibn Kathir endorses this and singles out one item: taking the disbelievers as friends is one of the categories of mischief on the earth (8:73; 4:144), and the ayah that follows warns that the hypocrites will be in the lowest depth of the Fire, with no helper (4:145).

What did they imagine they were doing? Ibn Kathir renders their meaning: "We seek to be friends with both parties, the believers and the disbelievers, and to have peace with both parties." Muhammad bin Isḥāq reported that Ibn ʿAbbās glossed it, "We seek to make amends between the believers and the People of the Book." Their sabotage wore the face of diplomacy. And Ibn Kathir makes a startling observation: since the outward appearance of the hypocrite displays belief, he confuses the true believers — so if the hypocrite simply remained a disbeliever rather than pretending, the evil resulting from him would be *less*. Better still, if he became sincere with Allah and made his statements conform to his deeds, he would gain success.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes the force of *innamā* in their reply — indicating not merely emphasis but exclusivity: *nothing but* reformers, so their activities could have nothing to do with disorder. Allah answers, *"Indeed, it is they who are the corruptors, but they do not perceive it,"* and two things follow: their activities really did produce disorder, and they were not even aware of the possibility. Some mischief everyone recognises — theft, robbery, murder — and every conscientious man refrains from it. But there is another kind that does not look like mischief from the outside and works unseen, destroying the morals of men and thereby opening the door to every kind of disorder. Oral claims settle nothing: what thief would call himself a thief? If a man's activities do result in mischief, he is a mischief-maker even if he had no such intention. So intention alone is not sufficient; far more essential is to orient oneself in thought and deed in harmony with the Sharīʿah, for an action may, despite the best intentions, result in disorder if it is not guided by the Sharīʿah. And Allah alone knows hearts and consequences: *"And Allah knows the one who makes mischief distinct from him who promotes good"* (2:220).

**"Shall we believe as the fools have believed?"** The invitation was to believe as the believers believe — Ibn Kathir spells it out: in Allah, His angels, His Books, His Messengers, resurrection after death, Paradise and Hellfire, and to obey Allah and His Messenger by heeding the commands and avoiding the prohibitions. By "the fools" — may Allah curse them for it — they meant the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. This is the reading of Abū al-ʿĀliyah, of as-Suddī in his Tafsir with a chain to Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Masʿūd and other Companions, and of ar-Rabīʿ bin Anas and ʿAbdur-Raḥmān bin Zayd bin Aslam. Ibn Kathir renders the sneer: "Us and them having the same status, following the same path, while they are fools?!"

He then explains the word. The fool, *safīh*, is the ignorant, simple-minded person who has little knowledge in areas of benefit and harm — which is why, according to the majority of the scholars, Allah used the term to include children in 4:5, where guardians are told not to hand over property to "the foolish." Then Allah returns the word to its owners: *"Indeed, it is they who are the fools, but they do not know."* Ibn Kathir's comment is piercing: since they are so thoroughly ignorant, they are unaware of their own degree of deviation and ignorance, and such a situation is more dangerous, a severer case of blindness, and further from the truth than that of one who is aware.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān takes this ayah as the criterion of true faith. By the consensus of the commentators, "the people" here are the Companions, since it is just these people who embraced faith and accepted the Qurʼān as the word of Allah while it was being revealed. Their faith is therefore the touchstone for every other Muslim's: any belief or deed that departs from their faith and practice — however pleasing in its looks, however good in its intention — is not valid according to the Sharīʿah. A man who presumes to interpret a doctrine or an ayah in a way that departs from the explicit explanation given by the Qurʼān itself or by the Prophet ﷺ, and then claims Islam on the strength of that interpretation, falls under *"they are not believers"* — even if he performs his religious duties exactly like the Muslims — until he agrees to conform to the criterion the Qurʼān has laid down. And Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a human observation: this has always been the way of those who go astray — anyone who tries to show them the right path is, in their eyes, ignorant and stupid. It also notes a telling detail: they could only have been this outspoken before the poor among the Muslims; otherwise they were very careful about keeping their disbelief concealed.

**"We were only mocking."** Ibn Kathir describes the two faces. When the hypocrites meet the believers they proclaim their faith and pretend to be believers, loyalists and friends, in order to misdirect, mislead and deceive them — and to have a share of whatever benefits and gains the believers might acquire. But when they are alone with "their *shayāṭīn*," meaning their devils, such as their leaders and masters among the rabbis of the Jews, the hypocrites and the idolators, they say, *"Truly, we are with you; verily, we were but mocking."* Muhammad bin Isḥāq reported that Ibn ʿAbbās glossed this as "we only mock people and deceive them"; aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, "we were mocking the Companions of Muhammad"; ar-Rabīʿ bin Anas and Qatadah said similarly. On the word itself, Ibn Jarīr said: "The devils of every creation are the mischievous among them. There are both human devils and Jinn devils" — citing 6:112, where every prophet is given enemies, devils among mankind and jinn, "inspiring one another with adorned speech as a delusion."

The answer to this claim needs care, and Ibn Kathir gives the classical explanation. Allah punishes them for their mockery using the same term for the deed and for its recompense, although the meaning is different — as in *"the recompense for an offence is an offence equal to it"* (42:40) and *"whoever transgresses against you, transgress likewise against him"* (2:194). The first act is an act of injustice; the second is an act of justice. Both carry the same name while being different in reality. Ibn Kathir states plainly that this is how the scholars explain deceit, cunning and mocking when these are attributed to Allah in the Qurʼān: Allah exacts revenge for certain evil acts with a punishment similar in nature to the act itself. And he affirms the consensus of the scholars that Allah does not do these things out of joyful play, but as a just form of punishment.

Ibn Jarīr locates part of the recompense on the Day of Resurrection, quoting 57:13 — the hypocrites, men and women, calling to the believers, "Wait for us! Let us get something from your light!" and being told, "Go back to your rear! Then seek a light!" while a wall is put up between them with a gate in it, mercy inside and torment outside — and 3:178, that the postponing of punishment is no good for the disbelievers, but lets them increase in sinfulness. "This, and its like," he said, "is Allah's mockery of the hypocrites and the people of Shirk."

## What they do not perceive

Three times the verdicts close on the same note — *they do not perceive it* (9), *they perceive not* (12), *they know not* (13) — and the last of the exchanges extends it into an image: *"and leaves them increasing in their transgression, wandering blindly."*

As-Suddī reported that Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Masʿūd and several other Companions said *yamudduhum* means **He gives them respite**; Mujāhid said it means He causes their deviation to increase. Ibn Kathir sets beside this Allah's word about those He augments with wealth and children: *"Do they think that by the wealth and the children with which We augment them, We hasten to give them with good things? Nay, but they perceive not"* (23:55–56). Ibn Jarīr judged the correct meaning of the ayah to be "We give them increase from the view of giving them respite and leaving them in their deviation and rebellion," and cited as a parallel *"And We shall turn their hearts and their eyes away, as they refused to believe in it the first time, and We shall leave them in their trespass to wander blindly"* (6:110).

*Ṭughyān* here means to transgress the limits — the same word Allah uses of the flood, "when the water rose beyond its limits, We carried you in the ship" (69:11): a picture of water breaking its banks. And of the blind wandering Ibn Jarīr said: "In the misguidance and disbelief that has encompassed them, causing them to be confused and unable to find a way out of it. This is because Allah has stamped their hearts, sealed them, and blinded their vision. Therefore, they do not recognize guidance or find the way out of their deviation."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders the mechanics plainly. They were mightily pleased with themselves, believing they could so easily make a fool of the Muslims and get away with it, while in fact they were only making fools of themselves. In His forbearance and mercy Allah gave them a long rope. Seeing no apparent sign of punishment descending, they were encouraged in their complacency and rebellion, until the cup of their iniquity was full — and one day they were caught.

## The trade that lost everything

The passage ends in the language of the marketplace: *"they purchased error with guidance, so their commerce was profitless, and they were not guided."*

In as-Suddī's Tafsir, Ibn ʿAbbās and Ibn Masʿūd said this means they pursued misguidance and abandoned guidance. Mujāhid said, "They believed and then disbelieved." Qatadah said, "They preferred deviation to guidance" — which Ibn Kathir likens to Allah's word about Thamūd, whom "We granted guidance, but they preferred blindness to guidance" (41:17). Summing up the scholars of Tafsir, Ibn Kathir says the hypocrites deviate from true guidance and prefer misguidance, substituting wickedness in place of righteousness — a meaning that includes those who first believed and then disbelieved, "therefore their hearts are sealed" (63:3), and also those who simply preferred deviation over guidance; the hypocrites, he notes, fall into several categories. And "their commerce was profitless, and they were not guided" means their trade did not succeed, nor were they righteous or rightly guided throughout any of it. Ibn Jarīr narrated Qatadah's lament on this ayah: "By Allah! I have seen them leaving guidance for deviation, leaving the Jamāʿah for the sects, leaving safety for fear, and the Sunnah for innovation."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lands the irony. These were worldly-wise men who had grown up in a pagan society and knew very well what the way of the disbelievers was; they had become familiar enough with Islam too, and could easily see the difference. Yet in their greed, for the sake of petty worldly profit, they bartered away something as invaluable as faith for something as worthless and even harmful as disbelief. By giving the name of *trade* to this action, the Qurʼān suggests that these shrewd operators had no understanding even of the art of trading.

## Living it

The passage is not a museum piece about one faction in Madinah; it hands the believer a set of tests.

**Watch the tongue first.** Ayah 10 attaches the grievous punishment to lying, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads that habit as the root from which hypocrisy and disbelief grew — which is why the Qurʼān names it in the same breath as idolatry. Habitual untruth is not a small matter; on this reading it is where the larger ruin starts.

**Measure faith against the Companions, not against your own taste.** Ayah 13 makes their faith the touchstone. However pleasing a reinterpretation looks, and however good the intention behind it, what departs from the faith and practice of the Companions is not valid in the Sharīʿah.

**Do not trust the label "reform."** Ayat 11–12 warn that some corruption arrives insisting it is *nothing but* peace-making, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is explicit that sincere intention does not sanctify an action out of step with the Sharīʿah — an action may result in disorder despite the best intentions if it is not guided by it.

**Fear the ruin you cannot feel.** The verdicts keep closing on *they do not perceive*, *they do not know*, and Ibn Kathir says this unawareness is exactly what makes their case more dangerous, a severer blindness, and further from the truth than that of a man who knows. The remedy is the one Ibn Kathir names while the door is still open: whoever becomes sincere with Allah and makes the statements he utters conform to his deeds will gain success.

passages.title: Two parables of the hypocrites: fire and storm
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat bring the portrait of the hypocrites in Sūrat al-Baqarah to a close with two extended comparisons — one of a fire that goes out, one of travellers caught in a thunderstorm. What holds them together is a single image: **light**. In the first, light is found and then lost; in the second, it is sometimes lit and sometimes extinguished.

## Where these ayat sit

Ibn Kathir steps back here and sorts people into types. The believers are those described in the first four ayat of al-Baqarah (2:2–5); the disbelievers in the two that follow; and then come the hypocrites. And the hypocrites, he says, are not one thing. There are **the complete hypocrites, mentioned in the parable of the fire**, and **the hesitant hypocrites, whose light of faith is sometimes lit and sometimes extinguished** — the parable of the rain was revealed about this category, which, he adds, "is not as evil as the first category."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the same line in human terms. On the one hand were people in whom disbelief had taken deep roots, so that they had little inclination towards Islam but pretended to be Muslims for worldly motives — these are the man who, having found light, again loses it and is left in darkness. On the other hand were people who did recognise the truth of Islam and sometimes wished to be genuine Muslims, but whose worldly interests would not allow it, so that they remained in a perpetual state of hesitation and doubt — these are the men caught in a thunderstorm, who move forward a step or two when there is a flash of lightning, but when it is over get stuck again.

## The first parable: a fire that goes out (ayat 17–18)

Ayah 17 sets a scene of relief. Someone kindles a fire. Ibn Kathir describes what follows: when the fire was lit and illuminated the surrounding area, **the person benefited from it and felt safe**. That is the whole point — this was not a stranger to light. He had it, and was helped by it.

Then, in Ibn Kathir's words, "the fire was suddenly extinguished. Therefore, total darkness covered this person, and he became unable to see anything or find his way out of it."

The ayah's own wording puts the loss as an act of Allah: **"Allah removed their light."** Ibn Kathir explains this to mean that Allah removed what benefits them — that is the light — and left them with what harms them, that is, the darkness and the smoke.

And the darkness itself — **ẓulumāt** — Ibn Kathir glosses in a single phrase: **"their doubts, disbelief and hypocrisy."** So the dark the man is left standing in is not merely an absence of information; it is what his own doubt and pretence have made of him. **"So they could not see"** (*lā yubṣirūn*) means, in Ibn Kathir's words, that they are unable to find the correct path or find its direction. They are not merely lost; they have lost the sense of which way to face.

**Ayah 18** then names three faculties, and Ibn Kathir takes them one by one: **ṣummun** — deaf, and thus cannot hear the guidance; **bukmun** — dumb, and cannot utter the words that might benefit them; **ʿumyun** — blind, in total darkness and deviation. And the blindness he describes goes beyond a missing lamp: this person **became so blind that even if there were light, he would not be able to see**. Alongside it he sets Allah's words in another sūrah: "Verily, it is not the eyes that grow blind, but it is the hearts which are in the breasts that grow blind" (22:46).

Hence the closing clause, **"so they return not."** Ibn Kathir explains that this is why he cannot return to the state that he was in before this happened to him — and such is the case with the hypocrites, who preferred misguidance over guidance and cannot get back to the state of guidance they were in, **since they sold it for misguidance**. And he draws a conclusion many readers miss: this parable indicates that the hypocrites **first believed, then disbelieved**. The fire was really lit. That is the tragedy of it.

## The second parable: caught in the storm (ayat 19–20)

Ayah 19 changes the weather. This, Ibn Kathir says, is another parable given about the hypocrites who sometimes know the truth and doubt it at other times.

**Ṣayyib** — Ibn Kathir reports that it means "the rain," as confirmed by Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿAbbās and several other Companions, as well as Abū al-ʿĀliyah, Mujāhid, Saʿīd bin Jubayr, ʿAṭāʾ, al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, Qatādah, ʿAṭiyyah al-ʿAwfī, ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurāsānī, as-Suddī and ar-Rabīʿ bin Anas. Ad-Daḥḥāk said it means the clouds; Ibn Kathir notes that the most accepted opinion is that it means the rain.

He then decodes each element of the storm:

- **The darkness (ẓulumāt)** — again "the doubts, disbelief and hypocrisy."
- **The thunder (raʿd)** — that which "shocks the hearts with fear." The hypocrites, Ibn Kathir says, are usually full of fear and anxiety, and he cites Allah's own description of them: "They think that every cry is against them" (63:4), and "They swear by Allah that they are truly of you while they are not of you, but they are a people who are afraid. Should they find refuge, or caves, or a place of concealment, they would turn straightway thereto in a swift rush" (9:56–57).
- **The lightning (barq)** — "is in reference to **the light of faith that is sometimes felt in the hearts of the hypocrites**."

So the storm holds both: a thunder that terrifies them, and a flash that is the light of faith visiting a heart that will not keep it.

They thrust their fingers in their ears against the stunning thunderclap "for fear of death" — and the ayah answers that panic at once: **"But Allah ever encompasses the disbelievers."** Ibn Kathir explains: their cautiousness does not benefit them, because they are bound by Allah's all-encompassing will and decision. He places beside it: "Has the story reached you of two hosts, of Firʿawn and Thamūd? Nay! The disbelievers persisted in denying. And Allah encompasses them from behind!" (85:17–20). Fingers in the ears are no defence against the One who encompasses them.

**Ayah 20** brings the flash right up to the eye: "The lightning almost snatches away their sight." Ibn Kathir gives two reasons at once — because the lightning is strong in itself, **and** because their comprehension is weak and does not allow them to embrace the faith. ʿAlī bin Abī Ṭalḥah reported that Ibn ʿAbbās commented on this ayah: "The Qur'an mentioned almost all of the secrets of the hypocrites."

Then the walking and the standing still. ʿAlī bin Abī Ṭalḥah also narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās on "Whenever it flashes for them, they walk therein": **"Whenever the hypocrites acquire a share in the victories of Islam, they are content with this share. Whenever Islam suffers a calamity, they are ready to revert to disbelief."** Ibn Kathir sets alongside it: "And among mankind is he who worships Allah on the edge: if good befalls him, he is content with that" (22:11).

Muḥammad bin Isḥāq reported another comment of Ibn ʿAbbās on the same words: "They recognise the truth and speak about it. So their speech is upright, but when they revert to disbelief, they again fall into confusion." Abū al-ʿĀliyah, al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, Qatādah, ar-Rabīʿ bin Anas and as-Suddī said the same, narrating it from the Companions, and Ibn Kathir judges this "the most obvious and most correct view, and Allah knows best."

## The flickering light on the Day of Judgment

From the walking and the stopping Ibn Kathir moves straight on — "consequently," he says — to the Day of Judgment, where the believers will be given a light **according to the degree of their faith**. Some will gain light that illuminates over a distance of several miles, some more, some less. Some people's light will glow sometimes and be extinguished at other times; they will therefore walk on the Ṣirāṭ — the bridge over the Fire — in the light, stopping when it is extinguished. And some will have no light at all: the hypocrites, of whom Allah says, "On the Day when the hypocrites — men and women — will say to the believers: 'Wait for us! Let us get something from your light!' It will be said to them: 'Go back to your rear! Then seek a light!'" (57:13).

Against this Ibn Kathir sets the believers: "their light running forward before them and by their right hands" (57:12), and their prayer, "Our Lord! Keep perfect our light for us, and grant us forgiveness. Verily, You are Able to do all things" (66:8).

Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated that ʿAbdullāh bin Masʿūd said of "their light will run forward before them": "They will pass on the Ṣirāṭ according to their deeds. The light that some people have will be as big as a mountain, while the light of others will be as big as a date tree. The people who will have the least light are those whose index fingers will sometimes be lit and extinguished at other times."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim also reported Ibn ʿAbbās saying that every person among the people of tawḥīd will gain a light on the Day of Resurrection, while the hypocrite's light will be extinguished — and when the believers witness that, they will feel anxious, and so they will supplicate, "Our Lord! Keep perfect our light for us." Ad-Daḥḥāk bin Muzāḥim said the same, adding that this happens when they arrive at the Ṣirāṭ. That prayer, then, is born at the edge of the Fire, out of the fright of watching someone else's lamp go out.

## Two parables — one type or two?

The scholars genuinely differed here, and Ibn Kathir lays out the difference honestly.

**Ibn Jarīr and several other scholars of tafsīr** stated that the two parables are about the same kind of hypocrite, so that the "or" in "**or** like a rainstorm from the sky" means "and" — just as in the ayah "And obey neither a sinner or a disbeliever among them." On this reading, the "or" offers a choice of using either example for the hypocrites. **Al-Qurṭubī** said the "or" is there "to show compatibility of the two choices, just as when one says, 'Sit with al-Ḥasan or Ibn Sīrīn'"; and on **az-Zamakhsharī's** view, each of these is the same as the other, so the meaning of "or" becomes "either" — both examples perfectly describe them.

**Ibn Kathir himself** — "I say," he writes — holds that these descriptions are related to the *type* of hypocrite, because there is a difference between them. He points out that Allah mentioned these types in Sūrat Barāʾah when He repeated "And among them" three times, describing their types, characteristics, statements and deeds; and that the two parables in Sūrat an-Nūr (24:39 and 24:40) likewise separate the advocates of disbelief from their followers.

## Hearts, and what grows in them

Ibn Kathir notes that just as the believers and the disbelievers each fall into two kinds, so the hypocrites are divided into two types: pure hypocrites, and those who have some hypocrisy in them. And to that second type he brings two hadith.

**The Two Sahihs record** that ʿAbdullāh bin ʿAmr said that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever has the following three characteristics will be a pure hypocrite, and whoever has one of the following three characteristics will have one characteristic of hypocrisy, unless and until he gives it up: whenever he speaks, he tells a lie; whenever he makes a covenant, he proves treacherous; whenever he is entrusted, he breaches the trust." From this Ibn Kathir concludes that a person might have both a part of faith and a part of hypocrisy — whether in deed, as this hadith stipulates, or in creed, as ayah 20 stipulates.

**Imām Aḥmad recorded** Abū Saʿīd saying that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that the hearts are of four types: a polished heart, as shiny as a radiating lamp — the heart of the believer, and the lamp is the light of faith; a sealed heart with a knot tied around its seal — the heart of the disbeliever; a heart that is turned upside down — the heart of the pure hypocrite, "because he had knowledge but denied it"; and a wrapped heart, containing both belief and hypocrisy, in which faith is like a herb sustained by pure water and hypocrisy is like an ulcer that thrives on pus and blood — **"whichever of the two substances has the upper hand, it will have the upper hand on that heart."** Ibn Kathir notes that this hadith has a *jayyid ḥasan* (good) chain of narration.

## The closing warning

Ayah 20 ends: "And if Allah willed, He could have taken away their hearing and their sight. Certainly, Allah has power over all things."
