# Ayat 34–39: The refusal, the fall, and the return

**What this passage is about.** The previous ayat showed the angels learning that Adam possessed the knowledge needed for the office of vicegerency, and that they did not. Now, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, Allah willed to manifest that superiority in a visible and concrete form — so He commanded the angels to prostrate before Adam in his honour. What follows is a single unbroken story told in six ayat: an honour given, a refusal that ends in ruin, a home granted, a boundary crossed, a repentance accepted, and finally a rule laid down for every one of Adam's children. Two creatures fail in this passage, and they fail in opposite ways. Watch how each one answers for his failure — the whole passage turns on that.

## Ayah 34: the honour made visible, and the first sin ever committed

Ibn Kathir opens by saying that this ayah mentions the great honour Allah granted Adam, and that Allah reminded Adam's offspring of this fact. He notes the report of Musa's supplication — "O my Lord! Show me Adam who caused us and himself to be thrown out of Paradise" — and that when Musa met Adam he said to him, "Are you Adam whom Allah created with His Own Hands, blew life into and commanded the angels to prostrate before?"

**Was the command only to the angels?** The wording addresses the angels. But, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out, the fact that Iblis is the one excepted also suggests the command was given to all the created beings then in existence that possessed understanding, jinn as well as angels. The Qur'an mentions the angels alone because when superior beings like the angels were required to show respect for Adam, it goes without saying that lesser creatures were ordered to do the same.

**Iblis was not an angel.** Ibn Kathir is clear that Iblis was included in the command although he was not an angel; he "was trying — and pretending — to imitate the angels' behavior and deeds," and this is why the command took him in. Ibn Kathir points to Allah's words, *"Except Iblis. He was one of the Jinn; he disobeyed the command of his Lord"* (18:50). Muhammad bin Ishaq reported from Ibn ʿAbbas: "Before he undertook the path of sin, Iblis was with the angels and was called ʿAzazil. He was among the residents of the earth and was one of the most active worshippers and knowledgeable persons among the angels. This fact caused him to be arrogant. Iblis was from a genus called Jinn." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that his attainment in knowledge earned him the title *Ṭāʾūs al-Malāʾikah*, "the Peacock among the angels."

Sit with that for a moment. The first being to be expelled from the mercy of Allah was not an ignorant one. He was among the most active worshippers and the most knowledgeable — and, as Ibn ʿAbbas says, that is exactly the fact that made him arrogant.

**Prostration to Adam, obedience to Allah.** Qatadah's comment settles what might otherwise trouble a reader: "The obedience was for Allah and the prostration was before Adam. Allah honored Adam and commanded the angels to prostrate before him." Ibn Kathir also reports that some said this prostration was just a prostration of greeting, peace and honour, citing Yusuf's story, *"And he raised his parents to the throne and they fell down before him prostrate"* (12:100). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān argues the same point from the other side: such a prostration evidently cannot have been intended as an act of worship, since worshipping anyone other than Allah is *shirk* (associating partners with Allah) and *kufr* (disbelief), and no Sharīʿah could possibly permit it. In the days of the ancient prophets, then, prostrating before someone appears to have been an act of courtesy or respect, holding roughly the value that a greeting, a handshake or standing up in someone's honour holds for us.

**And is such a prostration allowed now? No.** Ibn Kathir notes the practice was allowed for previous nations but repealed for ours. Muʿadh said to the Prophet ﷺ that he had visited Ash-Sham and found the people there prostrating before their priests and scholars, and that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was more deserving of prostration. The Prophet ﷺ answered: *"No. If I was to command any human to prostrate before another human, I would command the wife to prostrate before her husband because of the enormity of his right on her."* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports that this narration has come down through twenty Companions, and notes that by the standard of *Tadrīb al-Rāwī* — a well-known work on the principles of hadith science — a report transmitted by as few as ten Companions is *mutawātir* (mass-transmitted), and enjoys the same authority in matters of ruling as the Qur'an itself.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the wisdom behind the repeal. Some acts are not shirk or disbelief in themselves, but may, through people's ignorance or thoughtlessness, become a prelude to them. The Sharīʿahs of the earlier prophets did not forbid such acts absolutely, but guarded them from being turned into instruments of shirk — and the practice of prostrating in respect did in time open that very door, causing distortions that later prophets had to rectify. Because the Prophet ﷺ is the last of the prophets and his Sharīʿah must remain valid until the end of time, Allah has stopped every chink through which idolatry could enter. Imam Al-Jassas states in *Aḥkām al-Qurʼān* that while it was permissible in the Sharīʿah of the earlier prophets to prostrate in honour of one's elders, our Sharīʿah has forbidden prostrating, bowing very low, or standing with one hand placed on the other in the manner of Salah before anyone — anything that might suggest worship — and has allowed only *salām* (greeting) and a handshake as a gesture of courtesy. The same principle explains other prohibitions: making pictures of living things, offering Salah at the hours the idolaters reserved for worshipping their gods, and — in a hadith reported by Muslim — a master calling his slave *ʿabd* or a slave calling his master *rabb*. The words themselves are harmless; they can be misconstrued. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that of Salah's four actions, standing and sitting are things one does habitually in daily life, while bowing and prostrating are not — which is why the Sharīʿah has identified those two with worship and reserved them for Allah alone.

**Why Iblis's refusal was disbelief.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises the obvious question: by the Sharīʿah, giving up an obligation in practice is a sin and a transgression, not infidelity — so why is Iblis described as an infidel? Because he did not merely fail to act; he *defied and challenged* a divine commandment, and in refusing to prostrate he virtually said that in his own opinion Adam was not worthy of it. Qatadah puts the same thing in terms of the heart behind it: "Iblis, the enemy of Allah, envied Adam because Allah honored Adam. He said, 'I was created from fire, and he was created from clay.' Therefore, the first error ever committed was arrogance, for the enemy of Allah was too arrogant to prostrate before Adam." Ibn Kathir follows this with a hadith he says is recorded in the Sahih: *"No person who has the weight of a mustard seed of arrogance in his heart shall enter Paradise."* Iblis had disbelief, arrogance and rebellion, says Ibn Kathir, all of which caused him to be expelled from the holy presence of Allah, and from His mercy.

How does a being of such learning fall so far? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records the scholars' differing explanations: some say it was his pride and vanity that caused Allah to take back from him the wealth of knowledge and understanding, so that he came to act like an ignorant fool; others suggest his error was due to self-love and ambition. The commentary *Rūḥ al-Bayān* resolves the question by quoting a line of Arabic verse whose sense is that once the aid of Allah has been withdrawn from a man, he can no longer save himself from sins, and every effort he makes only pushes him farther into misguidance. The conclusion drawn there is worth memorising: **never be vain about your learning, your deeds, or even your faith** — for faith is valid only if it lasts till one's final breath and into the first stage of the journey to the other world.

Hold that thought until ayah 37. The same passage that shows us a learned creature ruined by self-regard will show us a human being saved by the exact opposite instinct.

## Ayah 35: the honour continued — a home, an ease, and one boundary

The honour of ayah 34 does not stop with the prostration. Ibn Kathir titles this next stage "Adam was honored again": Allah honoured Adam by commanding the angels to prostrate before him, and then allowed him to live and eat wherever and whatever he wished in Paradise. Al-Hafiz Abu Bakr bin Marduwyah reported that Abu Dharr asked, "O Messenger of Allah! Was Adam a Prophet?" and he ﷺ said, *"Yes. He was a Prophet and a Messenger to whom Allah spoke directly"* — the direct address of this very ayah being what that refers to.

Ibn Kathir cites Muhammad bin Ishaq that this ayah indicates Hawwaʼ was created before Adam entered Paradise: after Adam had informed the angels of the names, he fell asleep, and Allah took one of his left ribs and made flesh grow in its place while he slept unaware, creating from it his wife, so that she could be a comfort for him. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that some scholars concluded from the sequence of events that Adam's creation and the angels' prostration took place somewhere outside Paradise and that he was sent there afterwards — though, it adds, the words of the Qur'an do not exclude the reading that both events took place in Paradise and he was simply not told until later where he was to live.

The word Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lingers on is **raghadan** (رَغَدًا): provision for which one does not have to work, and which is never exhausted nor falls short. Their life was totally free from all care.

Notice too how the grammar shifts. "Dwell" is not addressed to both of them but to Adam — *"you and your wife"* — while "eat" is in the **dual**: *kulā*, "eat, both of you." From this the jurists derive two principles: that the husband is responsible for providing the dwelling-place and the wife lives in the house her husband lives in, while in the matter of food the wife is not subservient to him — she eats whatever she needs or likes, as he does. "Wherever you will" shows that a person has the right to move freely from place to place according to his needs. And the verb *uskun*, "live," suggests a stay that was temporary, not permanent: Allah did not say Paradise had been given to them, only that they should live there. From this the *fuqahāʼ* (jurists) derive that if a man asks someone to live in his house, the other man does not thereby acquire ownership of it or a right to stay permanently. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that the right to *own* a dwelling-place in Paradise is earned through faith and good deeds, and can be acquired only after the Day of Judgement.

Then the one boundary. Allah did not want them to eat the fruit of a certain tree, but as a precautionary measure commanded them not to approach it even. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that this is where the jurists derive one of the basic principles of Islamic law: things or actions likely to serve as a means to a sin, or as its instruments, are equally forbidden — not forbidden in themselves, but forbidden because of what they lead to. It is the same principle we just met in the repeal of prostration; the Sharīʿah guards the road, not merely the destination.

**Which tree was it?** Ibn Kathir lists the conflicting opinions — grape, barley, date, fig; a tree whoever eats from is relieved of the call of nature; a tree the angels eat from so that they live for eternity — and then quotes Imam Abu Jaʿfar bin Jarir: "The correct opinion is that Allah forbade Adam and his wife from eating from a certain tree in Paradise, but they ate from it. We do not know which tree that was, because Allah has not mentioned anything in the Qur'an or the authentic Sunnah about the nature of this tree… Yet, this is knowledge that does not bring any benefit, just as being ignorant in its nature does no harm. Allah knows best." Ibn Kathir notes Ar-Razi stated something similar in his Tafsir, and calls this the correct opinion. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān agrees: some commentators say wheat, others a fig-tree or a grape-vine, but it is not really necessary to make specific what the Qur'an has left vague.

**Adam's lapse and the sinlessness of the prophets.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān treats this at length, because the seeming difficulty is real: Adam had been forbidden the tree and warned against his enemy, and yet he ate. There is an absolute consensus of the four great Imams of Islamic law and of all the authentic scholars that every prophet is innocent of and protected against all sins, major or minor; some have suggested prophets are not protected against minor sins, but the majority of authentic scholars do not agree. The reason is functional: prophets are sent as guides, and if a guide could go against Allah's commandments people would no longer trust his word or deed — and then the work of spiritual guidance becomes impossible. So what happened here? According to the consensus of the authentic scholars, a prophet's error always comes about through a misunderstanding or simple forgetfulness, never as a deliberate and wilful transgression. It is like the mistake of a *mujtahid* — a scholar qualified to derive a ruling where no explicit text exists — who, if he errs, is still rewarded for the effort.

Commentators offer several readings of Adam's lapse. One: a particular tree was pointed out to him, but the ban was on the kind, not that single tree — much as the Prophet ﷺ held a piece of silk and some gold and said these two things were forbidden to the men of his Ummah, where obviously the ban was on silk and gold as such and not on those two pieces, though someone could imagine otherwise. Satan exploited that misunderstanding, assuring Adam on oath that as a well-wisher he would never advise anything harmful, and that the forbidden tree was a different one. Two: Satan may have suggested that the prohibition was only for a period, as infants are denied heavy food until they have grown, and that it had now been lifted. Three: Adam may simply have forgotten, which the ayah *"Adam forgot, and We did not find him steadfast"* (20:115) seems to support. The essential point is that he did not deliberately and wilfully disobey. But the station of the prophets is so exalted that even a small oversight in so great a man counts as a great error — which is why such slips are described in the Qur'an as "sins" and drew Allah's displeasure, although they are not sins in their nature.

## Ayat 36–37: the slip, the descent, and the words that came down

**Fa-azallahumā, "he made them slip."** Ibn Kathir gives two readings of *ʿanhā*, "therefrom." It may refer to Paradise — Satan led Adam and Hawwaʼ away from it, as ʿAsim bin Abi An-Najud recited it — or it may refer to the forbidden tree, in which case, as Al-Hasan and Qatadah said, "he tripped them," meaning he made them slip *because of* the tree. And *"got them out from that in which they were"* means, says Ibn Kathir, out of the clothes, the spacious dwelling and the comfortable sustenance of the previous ayah. Everything ayah 35 granted, this ayah withdraws.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notices that the enemy is renamed here and unpacks it. In the earlier episode the Qur'an said **Iblīs**, from the root *balas*, "to be disappointed" — one who has lost all hope of receiving the grace of Allah. Here it says **al-Shayṭān**, from *shaṭn*, "to be far away" — one who has been removed far from the mercy of Allah. Iblis is a proper name; *shaytan* is the name of a genus that includes men and jinn both, though when the Qur'an says *al-Shaytan* with the definite article it always refers to Iblis.

Two safeguards are added. First, the Qur'an says Satan "brought them out," while in actual fact they were brought out under **a divine command** — the act is attributed to Satan because he served as the means and intermediary. The words do not in the least imply that Satan had any power whatsoever to act on his own, so any dualism of two competing powers is entirely out of the question. Second, on how Satan reached them at all, after his own expulsion in ayah 34. Ibn Kathir reports that the majority held Shaytan was originally prohibited from entering Paradise but at times sneaked in secretly; that the Tawrah stated he hid inside the snake's mouth; that some said he led them astray on his way out; and that Az-Zamakhshari held he led them astray while he was on earth and they were still in the heavens. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān offers that he may never have met them at all but planted the suggestion in their minds from afar — a thing Satan can always do — or, being a jinn given powers denied to man, assumed the shape of a snake or something else and so got in; and it notes that since the Qur'an reports him swearing to them that he was one of their well-wishers (7:21), it apparently suggests he did meet them and speak to them face to face. Ibn Kathir, answering the same question, states that the Paradise Adam was in was in the heavens and not on the earth, as the majority of scholars assert.

**"Some of you enemies of some."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives both possibilities: if Satan had not yet been turned out of the skies, he is included in the address, and the meaning is that the enmity between him and Adam's family would continue on earth; if he had already been expelled, the addressees are Adam, Hawwaʼ and their progeny, and the meaning is a double punishment — banishment from Paradise, and then the grief of watching enmity arise among their own children. And the earth itself is only *"an enjoyment for a time"* — Ibn Kathir: dwelling, sustenance and limited life, until the commencement of the Day of Resurrection. They were told they would have to leave this dwelling-place too, which meant, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, that they would not find real peace of mind there.

Two narrations Ibn Kathir cites here are worth pausing over, because both are about the moment of the fall. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated that Ubayy bin Kaʿb said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that Allah created Adam tall, with thick hair, like a date tree with full branches; when he ate from the forbidden tree his covering fell off, and when he saw himself he ran away through Paradise until his hair caught in a tree. Ar-Rahman called to him: *"O Adam! Are you running away from Me?"* He said, *"No, O my Lord! But I am shy."* And Muslim and An-Nasaʼi recorded that Abu Hurayrah said the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"Friday is the best day on which the sun has risen. On Friday, Allah created Adam, admitted him into Paradise, and expelled him from it."* Al-Hakim recorded Ibn ʿAbbas saying Adam was allowed to reside in Paradise between the ʿAsr prayer and sunset, and commented that this is "Sahih according to the Two Shaykhs, but they did not include it in their collections."

**Then the turn.** *"Then Adam received from his Lord words, and He accepted his repentance."* Notice who moves first. Adam does not invent the words; he **receives** them from his Lord. The way back was itself a gift.

Ibn Kathir reports that a large group of the early authorities — Mujahid, Saʿid bin Jubayr, Abu Al-ʿAliyah, Ar-Rabiʿ bin Anas, Al-Hasan, Qatadah, Muhammad bin Kaʿb Al-Qurazi, Khalid bin Maʿdan, ʿAtaʼ Al-Khurasani and ʿAbdur-Rahman bin Zayd bin Aslam — explained these "words" by Allah's statement in 7:23: *"Our Lord! We have wronged ourselves. If You forgive us not, and bestow not upon us Your mercy, we shall certainly be of the losers."* No excuse, no blaming of the one who deceived them, no argument: only *we have wronged ourselves*, and then a complete throwing of oneself on Allah's forgiveness and mercy.

As-Suddi reports from Ibn ʿAbbas a second, moving explanation. Adam said, "O Lord! Did You not create me with Your Own Hands?" He said, "Yes." "And blow life into me?" "Yes." "And when I sneezed, You said, 'May Allah grant you His mercy.' Does not Your mercy precede Your anger?" He was told, "Yes." "And You destined me to commit this evil act?" "Yes." "If I repent, will You send me back to Paradise?" Allah said, "Yes." Al-Hakim recorded this in his *Mustadrak* from Ibn Jubayr from Ibn ʿAbbas, and said, "Its chain is Sahih and they did not record it."

Now set the two failures of this passage side by side, because this is the hinge of the whole passage. Iblis, confronted with his refusal, argued from his own superiority: *I was created from fire, and he was created from clay*. Adam, confronted with his slip, argued from nothing but his Lord's mercy: *does not Your mercy precede Your anger?* One appealed to himself. The other appealed to Allah. That, and not the size of the offence, is the difference between the one expelled from Allah's mercy and the one whose repentance was accepted.

Ibn Kathir explains the sealing words *"Verily, He is the One Who accepts repentance, the Most Merciful"* to mean that Allah forgives whoever regrets his error and returns to Him in repentance — as in *"Know they not that Allah accepts repentance from His servants"* (9:104) and *"whosoever repents and does righteous good deeds"* (25:71). These ayat, he says, testify that Allah forgives the sins of whoever repents, demonstrating His kindness and mercy towards His creation and servants.

## Ayat 38–39: the descent repeated — and the two roads out of it

Here is a detail easy to miss: the command to go down is issued **twice**, in ayah 36 and again here, with the repentance placed between them. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains why the order was not withdrawn even after Adam had been pardoned — **only the mode was now altered**. Earlier the command had been given in the mode of *authority*, and the sending down was intended as a punishment; hence the reference to enmity among men. Now it is in the mode of *wisdom*, and the sending down is an honour — the honour of vicegerency; hence the reference to the things vicegerency involves: revelation, guidance, and the promise attached to following it. The office announced before the prostration of ayah 34 is finally handed over here.

Ibn Kathir states that when Allah sent Adam, Hawwaʼ and Shaytan down to earth from Paradise, He warned them that He would reveal Books and send Prophets and Messengers to them, that is, to their offspring. Abu Al-ʿAliyah said *al-hudā*, the guidance, "refers to the Prophets, Messengers, the clear signs and plain explanation," and Ibn Kathir explains "whoever follows My guidance" as whoever accepts what is contained in Allah's Books and what He sends the Messengers with. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān glosses the guidance as the injunctions of the Sharīʿah, sent down through revelation.

**"No fear upon them, nor shall they grieve."** Ibn Kathir divides the two neatly: no fear regarding the Hereafter, no grief regarding the life of this world. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān defines them: *fear* is the anxiety one feels in apprehending some trouble or pain in the future; *grief* is the sorrow arising from the loss of something valuable, or from failing to attain something desired. Between them the two comprehend every possible form of comfort and peace — nothing ahead to dread, nothing behind to mourn.

Then a fine grammatical observation from Maʿārif ul Qurʼān. Of fear, the Qur'an speaks in general terms and uses a **noun**: *lā khawfun ʿalayhim*, literally "no fear upon them." Of grief it employs a **verb** with a pronoun placed before it as subject: *wa lā hum yaḥzanūn*, "they shall not grieve." The implication drawn is that being totally free from every sense of loss is possible only for the *awliyāʾ* — the friends of Allah, rendered only weakly by the English "saints" — those who follow the guidance in all its details, because they have annihilated their own desires and their very will in submitting themselves totally to the will of Allah. As for others, no man, whether an emperor or a billionaire, can help being grieved at the loss of something valued or at a frustrated desire; that is simply a necessary part of the scheme of things. The Qur'an itself reports the people of Paradise saying, *"All praise belongs to Allah who has put away all sorrow from us"* (35:34) — which means some degree of sorrow is inevitable for every human being except those who have perfected their relationship with Allah.

Two clarifications guard this from misreading. First, the negation applies only to the loss of worldly things and the frustration of worldly desires; as for anxiety about the next world, the fear of Allah and the deep sense of awe before His Glory, the friends of Allah are far ahead of other men. It has been reported that the Prophet ﷺ often appeared worried and in deep thought — not from any worldly fear or loss, but out of his anxiety for his Ummah and his awe before Divine Glory. Second, the ayah does not imply that prophets and righteous people feel no instinctive human fear before frightening things: the Qur'an relates that when Musa's staff turned into a dragon, *"Musa felt a fear in himself"* (20:67) — an instinctive, physical fear, which disappeared altogether when Allah said, *"Do not be afraid."*

Ibn Kathir sets this ayah beside its parallel in Ta Ha: *"whoever follows My guidance, he shall neither go astray, nor shall he be distressed"* (20:123), on which Ibn ʿAbbas commented, "He will not be misguided in this life or miserable in the Hereafter." And he pairs that with the opposite: *"whosoever turns away from My Reminder, verily, for him is a life of hardship, and We shall raise him up blind on the Day of Resurrection"* (20:124).

Which brings the passage to its last ayah — the road Iblis took, now opened to anyone who wants it. *"But those who disbelieve and deny Our signs — such are the dwellers of the Fire; they shall abide therein forever."* Ibn Kathir explains: they will remain in Hell for eternity and will not find a way out of it. Two things are named, not one — disbelief, and the denial of the signs — and that is precisely the posture the passage opened with, when a knowledgeable creature met a clear divine command and judged, by his own reckoning, that it did not deserve to be obeyed.

## What the passage asks of us

- **Guard the heart, not just the record.** Iblis had knowledge and long worship, and a mustard seed's weight of arrogance undid it. The first error ever committed was arrogance.
- **Take no confidence in your own learning, deeds, or even your faith** — as *Rūḥ al-Bayān* concludes — since faith is valid only if it lasts to the final breath.
- **Stay away from the edges.** Allah did not say "do not eat"; He said "do not go near." What leads to the sin is treated like the sin — the same principle by which our Sharīʿah closed the door on prostration to any creature.
- **When you slip, do what Adam did, not what Iblis did.** Own it — *we have wronged ourselves* — and appeal to nothing but the mercy of the One who accepts repentance.
- **Repentance restores the relationship even when it does not cancel the consequence.** Adam was forgiven and still went down to earth — but the second time the order came in the mode of wisdom, and the descent was an honour: the honour of vicegerency.
- **Follow the guidance that comes.** The whole human situation is summed up in ayah 38: exile with a promise attached. Fear and grief are lifted from those who take it; the Fire is named for those who turn away.

passages.title: Israel called to honour its covenant
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat open a long, direct address to the Jewish community of Madinah, and they move as one argument rather than four. Remember what Allah gave you; honour the covenant you made with Him; believe in this revelation, which confirms what you already hold; stop dressing truth in falsehood and stop hiding it; and then pray, give, and bow along with those who bow. One thread runs through all of it — *you of all people already know*. Knowledge of the favours, knowledge of the covenant, knowledge of the Prophet's ﷺ description written in their own Books. The passage begins with what they know and ends with what they must now do about it.

## Where the passage stands in the surah

Maʿārif ul Qurʾān sets the scene. Those who rejected the message in the Prophet's ﷺ time were of two very different sorts: the *mushrikīn*, the idolaters and associators, who had no religious learning, were mostly unlettered, and followed the customs of their forefathers — the people of Makkah in general, whom the Qur'an calls the *Ummiyyūn*, the unlettered; and, on the other hand, those who believed in earlier prophets and knew earlier revealed Books such as the Tawrāh and the Injīl, and were known as well-educated. Among these were the followers of Mūsā (peace be upon him) who did not accept ʿĪsā (peace be upon him) as a prophet — the Jews; and the followers of ʿĪsā (peace be upon him) who did not believe that Mūsā (peace be upon him), being a prophet, was divinely protected from sin — the Christians. Because of their belief in one or both of those Books, the Qur'an calls the two groups *Ahl al-Kitāb*, the People of the Book. Being educated, they were respected and trusted, their opinion carried real weight, and if they came to the straight path others could be expected to follow.

The Jews predominated in Madinah and its surroundings, and al-Baqarah is a Madinan surah. So, having dealt with the idolaters, it turns to the People of the Book in a special way, from ayah 40 through to ayah 123, in a persuasive and friendly tone: recalling the noble family they belong to and the honour they receive on account of it, recounting Allah's blessings on them, making them aware of their misdeeds, and inviting them to the straight path. All of this is said briefly first — an invitation to faith, then an invitation to good deeds — and our four ayat are that opening summary. The long, detailed address that follows is bracketed at both ends by the same words, *yā Banī Isrāʾīl*, "O children of Israel," repetition being the usual rhetorical device for making an appeal persuasive.

## The name that carries the argument

Ibn Kathir reads the opening call as an appeal to lineage. Allah commanded the Children of Israel to embrace Islam and to follow Muhammad ﷺ, reminding them of their father Israel — Allah's Prophet Yaʿqūb — as if to say: *O children of the pious, righteous servant of Allah who obeyed Allah! Be like your father, following the truth.* It is the same move as saying, "O son of the generous man, do this," or "O son of the scholar, seek knowledge" — and like Allah's own words, "O offspring of those whom We carried in the ship with Nūḥ! Verily, he was a grateful servant" (17:3).

That Israel is Yaʿqūb is established in a report Abu Dawud At-Tayalisi recorded from ʿAbdullah Ibn ʿAbbās: a group of Jews came to the Prophet ﷺ and he asked them, *"Do you know that Israel is Jacob?"* They said, "Yes, by Allah." He said, *"O Allah, be witness."*

And the name carries meaning. At-Tabari recorded from Ibn ʿAbbās that *Isrāʾīl* means "the servant of Allah"; Maʿārif adds that it is a Hebrew word with that sense, and that it is Yaʿqūb's second name — among the prophets, it notes, only the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ has several names, apart from Yaʿqūb (peace be upon him), who has two. So there is a reason the Qur'an addresses them here as "Children of Israel" rather than "Children of Yaʿqūb": the title reminds them that they are the children of *the servant of Allah*, and that they should follow their father's example in worshipping Allah alone and obeying Him. Before a single command is given, the name has already made the case.

## Two things to remember: the favour, and the covenant

Which favour? The early authorities filled it in from different angles. Mujāhid: that Allah made water gush from stones, sent down manna and quails, and saved them from being enslaved by Pharaoh. Abu al-ʿĀliyah: that He sent Prophets and Messengers among them and revealed Books to them. Ibn ʿAbbās, in a report of Muhammad bin Isḥāq: "My support for you and your fathers" — that is, saving them from Pharaoh and his people. Ibn Kathir notes the parallel with Mūsā's own words to them: Allah "made Prophets among you, made you kings, and gave you what He had not given to any other among the nations" (5:20) — meaning, in their time.

Maʿārif relays a fine observation from al-Qurṭubī here. When Allah calls the Israelites to worship and obey Him, He recounts the bounties He has showered on them; but to the followers of the Prophet ﷺ He says simply, "Remember Me, I will remember you" (2:152). It is a subtle suggestion of this Ummah's standing: it begins by recognising the Benefactor and through that knowledge recognises His gifts, whereas other peoples begin from the gifts and work back through them to the Giver.

Then the covenant: "Fulfil My covenant, I shall fulfil your covenant." Ibn Kathir explains it as *My covenant that I took from you concerning Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, when he is sent to you, so that I grant you what I promised you if you believe in him and follow him* — and Allah would then remove the chains and restrictions placed around their necks because of the errors they had committed. The scholars identified this covenant in more than one way, and the sources report the difference rather than settling it:

- **Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī** said it is the covenant of 5:12, where Allah took the covenant from the Children of Israel and appointed twelve leaders among them, saying: "I am with you if you perform aṣ-Ṣalāh and give Zakāh and believe in My Messengers, honour and assist them, and lend a good loan to Allah; verily I will expiate your sins and admit you to Gardens under which rivers flow." Maʿārif reports the same identification from Qatādah and Mujāhid, noting that this covenant is mentioned in the Tawrāh as well.
- **Other scholars** said it is what Allah took from them in the Tawrāh: that He would send a great Prophet — Muhammad ﷺ — from the offspring of Ismāʿīl, who would be obeyed by all peoples; so whoever obeys him, Allah forgives his sins, admits him to Paradise and awards him two rewards. Ibn Kathir mentions that ar-Rāzī gathered several cases of earlier Prophets bringing news of the coming of Muhammad ﷺ.
- **Abu al-ʿĀliyah** read it more broadly: "His covenant with His servants is to embrace Islam and to adhere to it."

Maʿārif harmonises them. The covenant of 5:12 mentions acts like prayer and alms, but its most important clause is faith in *all* of Allah's messengers, the Prophet ﷺ included — and so, according to Ibn ʿAbbās (via Ibn Jarīr), the covenant here signifies having faith in and obeying the Prophet ﷺ.

And Allah's side of the exchange? Ad-Ḍaḥḥāk reported from Ibn ʿAbbās that "I fulfil My obligations to you" means "I will be pleased with you and admit you into Paradise" — and as-Suddī, ad-Ḍaḥḥāk, Abu al-ʿĀliyah and ar-Rabīʿ bin Anas said the same. Maʿārif reaches the same place from 5:12: Allah will forgive the sins of those who keep the terms, and admit them to Paradise. Sit with the disproportion. A servant keeps his word; Allah's return is Paradise.

Then, "and fear Me alone." Ibn ʿAbbās: fear the punishment I might send upon you as I did upon your forefathers. Ibn Kathir notes the movement in the ayah — encouragement first, then warning — so that they might return to the truth, follow the Messenger ﷺ, heed the Qur'an's commands and prohibitions, and believe in what it contains.

## Act on what you already know

Everything after this rests on the same fact: they *knew*. What follows in ayat 41 and 42 is not really four separate commands but four faces of one demand.

**Believe in it, because it confirms what you hold.** "What I have sent down" is the Qur'an revealed to Muhammad ﷺ, the unlettered Arab Prophet — bringer of glad tidings, a warner and a light. It contains the truth from Allah and affirms what was revealed before it in the Tawrāh and the Injīl. Abu al-ʿĀliyah reads the ayah as: "O People of the Book, believe in what I sent down that conforms to what you have" — precisely because they find the description of Muhammad ﷺ recorded in their own Books; similar statements are attributed to Mujāhid, ar-Rabīʿ bin Anas and Qatādah. Maʿārif adds a needed clarification: what the Qur'an confirms about those Books is the fact that they are Books of Allah. Distortions introduced into them over time are no part of the original texts, so the question of confirming such passages does not arise.

**So do not be the first to disbelieve.** Ibn ʿAbbās: "Do not become the first to disbelieve in the Qur'an (or Muhammad ﷺ), while you have more knowledge of it than other people." Abu al-ʿĀliyah: do not be the first — meaning from among the People of the Book — to disbelieve in Muhammad ﷺ after hearing that he was sent as a Prophet; al-Ḥasan, as-Suddī and ar-Rabīʿ bin Anas are reported similarly. Ibn Jarīr held that "therein" refers to the Qur'an mentioned earlier in the ayah. Ibn Kathir says both readings are correct because they are inter-related: whoever disbelieves in the Qur'an has disbelieved in Muhammad ﷺ, and whoever disbelieves in him has disbelieved in the Qur'an.

But how "first," when Quraysh and the Arabs generally had already rejected him? Ibn Kathir answers precisely: the ayah is addressing the Children of Israel specifically, and the Jews of Madinah were the first among them to be reached by the Qur'an — so their disbelief would make them the first of the People of the Book to disbelieve in it. And why single out being first at all, when disbelief is the ultimate sin whether one is first or last? Because, Maʿārif answers, the one who denies first bears not only the sin of his own denial but the added burden of misleading everyone who follows his example, and so undergoes a multiple punishment. The principle runs both ways: whoever is in any way responsible for others falling into sin carries that sin along with them, and whoever helps others to a good deed receives its reward along with them — a point that verses of the Qur'an and the ahadith of the Prophet ﷺ stress repeatedly.

**And do not sell My signs for a small price.** Ibn Kathir: do not substitute faith in My verses and belief in My Prophet for the life of this world and its appetites, which are minute and bound to end. Maʿārif tells us exactly what was at stake. The Israelite scholars were afraid that if they told the truth in this matter they would go against public sentiment and lose both their followers and their income. That is the "small price" — and it is why these ayat urge them to speak the truth without fear, since Allah alone is worthy of being feared. The Arabic *āyāt* means both "signs" and "verses," and Maʿārif states the ruling plainly: it is forbidden to take money from people by misinterpreting or concealing the verses of the Book of Allah in order to please them or to serve their worldly interests. There is an absolute consensus of the Ummah on this point. (The separate question of whether one may take a wage for *teaching* the Qur'an is, Maʿārif notes, not what this ayah is about; the jurists differ over it on other grounds.)

**And do not dress the truth in falsehood, nor conceal it.** Ibn Kathir observes that Allah forbade two things here and, in doing so, commanded two: to make the truth known, and to explain it. Ad-Ḍaḥḥāk reports Ibn ʿAbbās on the first: "Do not mix the truth with falsehood and the facts with lies." Qatādah understood it as: do not mix Judaism and Christianity with Islam — "while you know" that the religion of Allah is Islam, and that these are innovations that did not come from Allah; al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī is reported similarly. On "nor conceal the truth while you know," Muhammad bin Isḥāq narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās: "Do not hide the knowledge that you have of My Messenger and what he was sent with. His description, which you know about, can be found written in the Books that you have." Ibn Kathir adds a second possible sense of "while you know": while you know the tremendous harm this will do to people, misguiding them and leading them to the Fire, because they will follow the falsehood you mixed into the truth.

Notice how tightly this binds to what came before. The knowledge that should have made them the *first* to believe is the same knowledge that made concealment possible. A gift held back curdles.

Maʿārif states the ruling: it is not permissible to blend truth and falsehood in a way that leaves the listener confused about what the truth is, and it is forbidden to conceal the truth out of fear or greed. It illustrates this with a story al-Qurṭubī relates from the *Musnad* of ad-Dārimī. The Umayyad Caliph Sulaymān ibn ʿAbd al-Malik, visiting Madinah, summoned Abu Ḥāzim, and Abu Ḥāzim answered every question without flattery — including, when pressed for his opinion of the Caliph himself, a blunt word about how his forefathers had taken power. Rebuked by a courtier for rudeness, he replied that he had said only what Allah commanded, for Allah has enjoined upon the scholars to make the truth clear to people and not conceal it — and he recited, "You shall make it clear to the people and not conceal it" (3:187). Asked earlier in that same conversation which is the best form of speech, he had already given the answer this ayah is asking for: "Speaking the truth plainly and unreservedly before the man who can harm you in some way or from whom you expect a favour." When the Caliph later sent him a hundred gold dinars, he sent them back.

## From knowing to doing

The passage now turns from faith to action. The earlier ayat were concerned with true faith and doctrine; ayah 43 speaks of good deeds, and names only the most important of them.

Maʿārif gives the diagnosis behind the prescription. It was usually the love of money and the love of power that made it difficult for the Jews, and especially for their scholars, to accept Islam — and the passage prescribes a remedy for the twin diseases: they should fortify themselves with *ṣabr* and *ṣalāh*. "Patience" is a weak translation of *ṣabr*, which carries three senses: bearing pain and misfortune patiently, restraining oneself from sin, and being steadfast in obeying Allah. In that wide sense it is the perfect remedy for love of money — because money is never an end in itself but only a means of satisfying appetites, so once a man firmly resolves not to follow his appetites like a slave, he no longer needs much money, nor will the love of it blind him to what is really gain and what is really loss. And *ṣalāh* is the remedy for ambition and the love of power, because outwardly and inwardly it is an exercise in humility: the more one tries to perform it properly, the more it purifies one of love of money and power, of ambition and pride. These being the real substance of spiritual disorder in a person, once they are brought under control it becomes easy to accept the truth and to stand firm in it.

Maʿārif is honest that the harder half of the remedy is the prayer. *Ṣabr* asks only that one give up excessive appetites, and the urge itself weakens within days. *Ṣalāh* asks for prescribed actions, at fixed hours, five times a day, and for the temporary renunciation even of perfectly lawful things — eating, drinking, speaking, walking. Why is that so heavy? Because the heart loves to roam freely through thought and fancy, and the limbs, being its servants, want the same freedom; prayer forbids exactly that. Motion is the disease, so the cure is its opposite: *khushūʿ*, which is usually rendered "humbleness of heart" but really means the restfulness of the heart. And since a mind cannot be emptied of thoughts by trying, but can be absorbed in one thought until the others fall away by themselves, the Qur'an supplies the thought to be absorbed in — that we are to meet our Lord and receive the reward of our obedience, and that we are to return to Him and give an account. Hope and fear together, and prayer stops being a burden.

**"Establish the prayer."** The prayer the Qur'an prescribes is not contemplation or meditation; in the terminology of the Sharīʿah, *ṣalāh* is a definite form of worship whose mode is divinely ordained. And almost every time the Qur'an commands it, it pairs it with *iqāmah*, which lexically means making a thing straight, or keeping it firmly in its place — and a thing standing straight and upright tends to last, so the word also carries "establishing," "making perpetual." The command is therefore not merely to *offer* prayer but to perform the five ordained prayers steadfastly, in the prescribed form, at the prescribed hours, fulfilling all the necessary conditions. This matters for reading verses like "Indeed the Salāh restrains from indecency and evil" (29:45): those fruits belong to prayer performed in the full sense of *iqāmah*. So if one sees people quite regular in their prayers yet indulging in immodest or even evil behaviour, one should have no misgivings about the truth of that verse — such people have indeed been praying, but they have not been observing the conditions of *iqāmah*.

**"And give the zakāh."** Lexically the word carries two senses: to purify, and to grow. And zakāh is not a tax levied by a state or a society; in the terminology of the Sharīʿah it is that portion of one's belongings which is set apart and spent in total accordance with the injunctions of the Sharīʿah. Maʿārif notes that this ayah, addressed to the Israelites, does not by itself prove that prayer and alms were obligatory for them before Islam — but 5:12, with its "if you perform Salāh and pay Zakāh," does show that both were obligatory for them, even if the outward forms differed.

**"And bow with those who bow."** Why single out *rukūʿ* from all the postures of prayer? Maʿārif gives two answers. First, it is a metonymy — a part standing for the whole — just as "the recitation of the Qur'an at dawn" (17:78) means the dawn prayer, and as *sajdah* is used in some hadith narrations for a whole unit of prayer or even the entire prayer; so the ayah means, offer prayer along with those who offer prayer. Second, and more pointedly: the form of ritual prayer ordained for the Israelites and others included prostration but not this particular bowing. *Rukūʿ* in this form is peculiar to the Islamic Salāh alone. So "those who bow" are unmistakably the members of the Muslim Ummah, and the ayah is in effect asking the Israelites to accept Islam and to pray alongside the Muslims. Ibn Kathir reports the same from Muqātil — the People of the Book are commanded to pray behind the Prophet ﷺ, to pay the zakāh to him, and to bow with those who bow among the Ummah of Muhammad ﷺ; Allah is commanding them to be *with*, and *among*, that Ummah. Ibn Kathir adds that the phrase also means: be among the believers in performing the best of the deeds they perform, foremost among them the prayer.

Read this way, the last ayah is not a change of subject at the end of a rebuke. It is where the whole passage has been heading. You know the truth — so stop selling it, stop blurring it, stop burying it, and come stand in the row.

## Praying in congregation — where the scholars differ

Ibn Kathir notes that many scholars took ayah 43 as proof that congregational prayer is obligatory (for men), and Maʿārif lays out the disagreement over just how binding that is.

**One view**, held by a large body of Companions, their successors and jurists of the Ummah, is that praying in congregation is *wājib* — necessary — and that abandoning it is a sin; some Companions went so far as to hold that praying alone without a valid excuse recognised by the Sharīʿah is not permissible. The literal sense of ayah 43 supports this, and so, they hold, do certain hadith narrations. A hadith reported by Abu Dawud says that for a man living near a mosque, prayer is permissible only in the mosque. Al-Qurṭubī cites a hadith from Ibn ʿAbbās that the Prophet ﷺ said: "The man who hears the call for the prayers but does not go to the mosque for the congregation has not offered his prayers at all, unless he has some valid excuse." On this basis Companions such as ʿAbdullah ibn Masʿūd and Abu Mūsā al-Ashʿarī ruled that a man who lives close enough to hear the call and stays away without excuse has not offered an acceptable prayer at home. (Maʿārif clarifies that "hearing the call" means the call of a man with an ordinary voice — not an extraordinarily loud one, and not one broadcast by a loudspeaker.)

**The majority view** among the Companions, their successors and later jurists is that the congregation is a *Sunnah muʾakkadah* — an emphasised Sunnah — and among these the most emphasised, coming very close to being necessary. On the basis of other verses and narrations they read the imperative "bow with those who bow" as intended for emphasis; and the narrations that seem to forbid praying at home for those near a mosque, they take to mean that doing so is not the perfect way to pray.

Two reports from Imam Muslim frame it. From Abu Hurayrah: a blind Companion asked the Prophet ﷺ for permission to pray at home, since there was no one to take him to the mosque and bring him back. The Prophet ﷺ allowed him — then, as he was leaving, asked whether he could hear the call to prayer from his house. He said that he could. The Prophet ﷺ said: "In that case, you must come to the mosque." And from ʿAbdullah ibn Masʿūd, in what Maʿārif calls the most comprehensive statement on the matter: whoever wishes to meet Allah tomorrow as a true Muslim should offer these prayers regularly and steadfastly where the call to prayer is habitually made, for Allah laid down for the Prophet ﷺ certain ways of good guidance (*Sunan al-Hudā*), and praying the five prayers in congregation is one of them; whoever prays at home, keeping away from the congregation, has forsaken his Prophet's ﷺ Sunnah, and whoever forsakes that goes astray. He added that for every step a man takes to the mosque after purifying himself properly, Allah forgives him a sin, records him a good deed and raises him a rank — and that in their company, no one stayed away except those known for hypocrisy, so much so that a man too ill to walk would be carried to the mosque leaning on the shoulders of two men and stood in the row.

So the practical upshot, as Maʿārif draws it: a man who prays at home without a proper excuse such as illness has offered a valid prayer, but has given up an emphasised Sunnah and earned Allah's displeasure for it; and if he makes a habit of neglecting the congregation, he commits a grave sin.

## What the passage asks of us

The address is to the Children of Israel, but the obligations it names are ours, and it is worth taking them in the order the passage gives them.

Maʿārif draws a general ruling straight out of ayah 40: it is obligatory to fulfil an agreement one has entered into, and forbidden to break one's promise — the injunction stated explicitly in "Fulfil your agreements" (5:1). And according to a hadith reported by Muslim, those who break their promises will, before their final punishment in the next world, be humiliated before the whole human race when it assembles on the Day of Judgment: a flag will be placed as a mark beside every person guilty of this, and the bigger the crime, the higher the flag.

Then the rest follows the same logic. Do not let what you know be shaped by what you stand to lose. Do not blend a little falsehood into the truth until people can no longer tell where one ends and the other begins, and do not sit on knowledge that others need. And take the two positive commands as cure rather than burden — patience that loosens money's grip, an established prayer that keeps humbling you, and wealth given as Allah prescribed, which purifies what remains.

Ibn Kathir, commenting on the closing words of ayah 41 — "and have Taqwā of Me and Me alone" — reports from Ibn Abi Hatim that Ṭalq bin Ḥabīb said: "Taqwā is to work in Allah's obedience, on a light from Allah, hoping in Allah's mercy, and to avoid Allah's disobedience, on a light from Allah, fearing Allah's punishment." Not blind fear and not blind hope, but obedience with insight and restraint with insight. It is a fitting note for a passage addressed to people whose problem was never that they lacked light.

passages.tafsir:
These three ayat set a warning beside a remedy. Ayah 44 exposes a sickness in the religious leadership of the People of the Book: they urged others toward righteousness while forgetting themselves, even as they read the Scripture that condemned exactly that. Ayat 45 and 46 name two supports — patience and prayer — and the quality of heart that makes them light: hearts humbled before Allah, certain they are going to meet Him. Read together, as the passage is presented here, the warning and the supports belong to one subject: knowing, and doing.

## Ayah 44: preaching what you do not practise

**Who is addressed.** Ibn Kathir reads the verse as Allah's address to the People of the Book: "How is it, O People of the Book, that you command people to perform *Al-Birr* … yet forget yourselves and do not heed what you call others to?" ʿAbd al-Razzaq said that Maʿmar stated that Qatadah commented that the Children of Israel "used to command people to obey Allah, fear Him and perform *Al-Birr*. Yet, they contradicted these orders"; As-Suddi said similarly. Ibn Jurayj widened it: the verse "is about the People of the Book and the hypocrites. They used to command people to pray and fast. However, they did not practice what they commanded others" — and he drew the lesson for everyone: "So whoever commands people to do righteousness, let him be among the first of them to implement that command."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sharpens the picture: the Jewish scholars would advise friends and relatives to follow the Holy Prophet ﷺ and be steadfast in Islamic faith — which shows they themselves regarded Islam as the true faith — yet, enslaved to their desires, were not prepared to accept it themselves, though they were regular readers of the Torah and knew how emphatically it denounces the scholar who does not act upon his knowledge. And though the verse is outwardly addressed to those scholars, Maʿārif notes that in a larger sense it condemns all who preach good deeds to others but do not act on the principle themselves, who ask others to fear Allah but show no such fear in their own behaviour.

**"Al-Birr."** The word is not narrow: Ibn Kathir says it "encompasses all types of righteousness" — piety, righteousness, and every act of obedience to Allah. The contradiction is not one neglected duty; it is a whole life of instruction contradicted by a whole life of conduct.

**"And you forget yourselves."** Ibn ʿAbbas, in the narration of Muhammad ibn Ishaq, explains it simply: "You forget to practice it yourselves." He then adds a sharper layer, tied to the covenant themes running through this part of the surah: they forbade people from rejecting the prophethood and the covenant mentioned with them in the Tawrah, while they themselves had forgotten it — *"you have forgotten the covenant that I made with you that you will accept My Messenger. You have breeched My covenant, and rejected what you know is in My Book."* Their preaching pointed at the very truth their lives refused.

**"While you recite the Scripture."** This removes every excuse: they read Allah's Book, Ibn Kathir notes, and so "know what it promises to those who do not fulfill Allah's commandments." The closing rebuke — "Have you then no sense?" — is a call to see "what you are doing to yourselves, so that you might become aware of your slumber and restore your sight from blindness." The harm falls first on the preacher.

## This is not a verse against preaching

It would be easy to misread ayah 44 as telling flawed people to keep quiet. Ibn Kathir states otherwise outright: **Allah is not criticising the People of the Book for ordering righteousness**, because enjoining good is itself a part of righteousness and is an obligation for the scholars. What is required is that the scholar himself heed, and adhere to, what he invites others to — as Allah reports the words of the Prophet Shuʿayb: "I wish not, in contradiction to you, to do that which I forbid you. I only desire reform to the best of my power" (11:88). Ibn Kathir's conclusion: enjoining righteousness and performing righteousness are **both** required, and neither is rendered unnecessary by the practice of the other — "according to the most correct view of the scholars among the Salaf (predecessors) and the Khalaf (those who came after them)."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the same point, citing Rūḥ al-Maʿānī: doing a good deed is one form of virtue, and persuading others to do that good deed is another form of virtue in its own right; giving up the one does not mean one should give up the other. A man who does not offer his prescribed Salah has no reason to give up fasting too — nor does his failing argue that he should not be allowed to ask others to pray. Likewise, doing something the Shariʿah prohibits is one kind of sin, and failing to dissuade those one can influence from that misdeed is another kind; committing the one does not entail committing the other. Imam Malik cites Saʿīd ibn Jubayr: if everyone refused to counsel others on the assumption that he has no right to preach until he has purged himself of all sin, there would be no one left to give good counsel — for who can be totally free of sins? Hasan al-Basri said this is exactly what Satan wants: that people, obsessed by this false notion of purity, neglect their obligation to give religious instruction and good counsel to others. (Maʿārif cites Qurtubi.) Maulana Ashraf ʿAli Thanavi turned the problem inside out: on becoming aware of a certain bad habit in himself, he would expressly denounce that very tendency in his sermons, so that the *barakah* (blessing) of the sermon should help him get rid of it.

So, as Maʿārif sums up: ayah 44 does not imply that a man who has been indifferent to good deeds in his own life may not preach; it says that **the man who preaches should not neglect good deeds in his own life.**

**Why single out the preacher?** Such negligence is impermissible for preacher and non-preacher alike, but Maʿārif answers that the preacher's crime is the more serious: he commits it knowing it is a crime and cannot plead ignorance as an excuse, whereas the non-preacher — especially if he is illiterate — may to a certain degree plead ignorance of the law. Moreover, if a scholar or preacher commits a sin, he is in effect mocking at the Shariʿah. Anas reports from the Holy Prophet ﷺ that on the Day of Judgment Allah will forgive illiterate and ignorant people much more readily than He will the scholars.

## From the Sunnah: the weight of the contradiction

Imam Ahmad reported that Abu Waʼil said that while he was riding behind Usamah, Usamah was asked, "Why not advise ʿUthman?" He answered that he advised him in secret, that he would not start something he would hate to be the first to start, and that he would not say to a man, "You are the best man," even if he were his leader — because of what he had heard from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ:

> "A man will be brought on the Day of Resurrection and thrown in the Fire. His intestines will fall out and he will continue circling pulling them behind him, just as the donkey goes around the pole. The people of the Fire will go to that man and ask him, 'What happened to you? Did you not used to command us to do righteous acts and forbid us from committing evil?' He will say, 'Yes. I used to enjoin righteousness, but refrained from performing righteousness, and I used to forbid you to perform from evil while I myself did it.'"

Ibn Kathir notes this hadith was also recorded by **Al-Bukhari and Muslim**.

Ibrahim An-Nakhaʿi felt the weight of it: "I hesitate in advising people because of three Ayat" — of which the text before us quotes two: ayah 44, and "O you who believe! Why do you say that which you do not do? Most hateful it is to Allah that you say that which you do not do" (61:2–3).

Maʿārif adds two reports, citing Ibn Kathir. Anas reported that on the Night of the Ascension the Holy Prophet ﷺ passed by some people whose lips and tongues were being cut with scissors made of fire; asked who they were, Jibraʼil (peace be upon him) explained that they were certain avaricious preachers of the Holy Prophet's ﷺ Ummah who urged others to good deeds but ignored themselves. And in a report transmitted by Ibn ʿAsakir, certain people in Paradise will find acquaintances in the fire of Hell and ask them, "How is it that you find yourselves in hell, while we have attained Paradise just on account of the good deeds we had learnt from you"; those in Hell will reply: "We used to say all that with our tongues, but never acted upon what we said."

## Ayah 45: "Seek help through patience and prayer"

Now the remedy. Ibn Kathir: **Allah commanded His servants to use patience and prayer to acquire the good of this life and the Hereafter.**

**Ṣabr (patience)** is given more than one register:

- Muqatil ibn Hayyan read the ayah as "Utilize patience and the obligatory prayer in seeking the Hereafter," adding, "As for patience (here), they say that it means **fasting**." Similar texts are reported from Mujahid. Al-Qurtubi and other scholars commented, "This is why Ramadan is called *the month of patience*," as is mentioned in the Hadith literature.
- It was also said that patience here means **refraining from evil** — and this, Ibn Kathir notes, is why patience is mentioned alongside the practice of acts of worship, especially and foremost the prayer. Restraint and devotion are the two halves of a religious life.
- Ibn Abi Hatim narrated that ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab said: "There are two types of patience: good patience when the disaster strikes, and a better patience while avoiding the prohibitions of Allah." Ibn Abi Hatim said Al-Hasan Al-Basri was reported to have said similarly. Note the ranking: enduring what wounds you is good; holding yourself back from what tempts you is better.

**Ṣalāh (prayer)** is, in Ibn Kathir's words, "one of the best means of assistance for firmly adhering to Allah's orders," and he cites: "perform As-Salah. Verily, As-Salah prevents from *Al-Faḥshāʼ* (great sins of every kind), and *Al-Munkar*" (29:45). A reader coming straight from ayah 44 may pause here: the remedy Allah names for a life drifting away from its own words is a prayer that itself restrains conduct.

**"And truly it is heavy."** What is "it"? Ibn Kathir reports the difference: the pronoun refers to **the prayer**, as Mujahid is reported to have said and as Ibn Jarir chose; but it is possible the pronoun refers to **the advice** — to observe patience and the prayer — mentioned in the same ayah. He sets alongside this second possibility places where a great counsel is granted only to a certain kind of person (28:80, said about Qarun; 41:34–35, on repelling evil with what is better) — meaning, he says, that such advice is only implemented by those who are patient and the fortunate.

Either way, the Qurʼan is honest: this is heavy and burdensome — *except* upon one kind of person. Of *al-khāshiʿīn*, Ibn ʿAbbas said, in the narration of Ibn Abi Talhah: "They are those who believe in what Allah has revealed."

## Khushūʿ: humbleness of the heart

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān devotes its main discussion of ayah 45 to this word. **Khushūʿ** — the humbleness of heart that the Holy Qurʼan and the Hadith speak of — connotes a restfulness of heart and humility arising out of awareness of Allah's majesty and of one's own insignificance in comparison to it. Once acquired, it shows its fruit in making obedience and submission to Allah easy and pleasant; sometimes it even shows in a man's bearing, for such a man is disciplined and polite, modest and humble, and seems "broken-hearted" — one who has lost all vanity and self-love.

But it cannot be manufactured from the outside in. If a man does not bear genuine humility and fear of Allah in his heart, then for all his external modesty and downcast looks he does not really possess khushūʿ; it is not even proper to display its signs deliberately. Seeing a young man sitting with his head bowed down, ʿUmar said: **"Raise your head! Humbleness of heart is in the heart."** Ibrahim Nakhaʿi said khushūʿ does not mean wearing rough clothes, eating coarse food and keeping the head bowed down; it is "to treat the high and the low alike in matters of truth, and to keep the heart free to devote itself entirely to Allah and to the performance of what Allah has made obligatory for you." Hasan al-Basri gave ʿUmar himself as the illustration: he would speak loudly enough to be heard whenever he spoke, walk swiftly whenever he walked, and strike forcefully whenever he struck a man — and he undoubtedly was a man of real humbleness of heart. To put on such looks deliberately, Maʿārif concludes, is a kind of self-delusion and a ruse of Satan; but a man who manifests them without knowing it can be excused. (Maʿārif cites Qurtubi.)

Maʿārif adds a fine distinction of root: *khushūʿ*, by its lexical root, is the lowering of the voice and of the glance when it is unfeigned and arises out of real modesty and fear of Allah (as in "Voices have been hushed," 20:108), whereas the near-synonym *khuḍūʿ* refers to the bodily posture that shows modesty and humility (as in "So their necks will stay humbled to it," 26:4).

**Is khushūʿ a condition for the validity of prayer?** Here the scholars genuinely differed. The texts press its importance hard: "And perform the prayer for the sake of My remembrance" (20:14) — and since forgetfulness is the opposite of remembrance, the man who becomes unmindful of Allah while offering Salah is not fulfilling the obligation of remembering Him; another verse says, "Do not be among the unmindful" (7:205). The Holy Prophet ﷺ said that the Salah simply means self-abasement and humility; another hadith says that if a man's prayers do not restrain him from immodesty and evil, he goes farther and farther away from Allah.

Having quoted such verses and ahadith in his *Iḥyāʼ al-ʿUlūm*, **Imam al-Ghazali** suggests that khushūʿ must then be a necessary condition for Salah and that its acceptability must depend on it — adding that according to the blessed Companion Muʿadh ibn Jabal, and jurists as great as Sufyan al-Thawri and Hasan al-Basri, Salah offered without khushūʿ is not valid. **The four great Imams of Islamic jurisprudence and most of the jurists** do not hold it to be a necessary condition: while considering khushūʿ to be the very essence of Salah, they say the only necessary condition in this respect is that while saying *Allahu Akbar* at the beginning of the prayers one turns with all one's heart to Allah, with the intention (*niyyah*) of praying for Allah's sake alone. If khushūʿ is not attained through the rest of the prayer, one gets no reward for that part — but from the point of view of *fiqh* (jurisprudence) one is not charged with having forsaken Salah, nor liable to the punishment meted out to those who give up prescribed prayers without a valid excuse.

Al-Ghazali explains the divergence: the *fuqahāʼ* (jurists) are not concerned with inner qualities and states of the heart (*aḥwāl*), but only enunciate the outward regulations of the Shariʿah on the basis of the external actions of men's physical organs — it does not lie within the jurisdiction of *fiqh* to decide whether one will be rewarded for a deed in the other world. Maʿārif adds a second explanation: the Qurʼan lays down that nothing is made obligatory for men beyond their endurance and power, and except for a few gifted individuals men in general are incapable of maintaining khushūʿ for the whole duration of the prayer. Al-Ghazali ends on mercy: one can depend on the infinite mercy of Allah and hope that the man who offers his prayers unmindfully will not be counted among those who give up prayer altogether — for he has tried to fulfil the obligation, and has been mindful of Allah alone at least while forming his intention. **Hope and fear are both involved here**: the fear of having incurred punishment, and the hope of being ultimately forgiven. So one should try one's best to be rid of laziness and indifference — but it is the mercy of Allah alone which can help one succeed in that effort.

## Ayah 46: the certainty that makes it light

Ayah 46 describes the *khāshiʿīn*: "those who are certain that they are going to meet their Lord, and that unto Him they are going to return." Ibn Kathir says this continues the subject that was started in the previous ayah — therefore the prayer, or the advice to observe it, is heavy *except* upon these.

**A word that carries its own opposite.** The Arabic is *yaẓunnūn*, from *ẓann*, which normally means supposing or thinking-likely. Ibn Jarir explains: "The Arabs call certainty as well as doubt, *Zann*. There are similar instances in the Arabic language where a subject as well as its opposite share the same name" — citing 18:53, where the criminals see the Fire and *ẓannū*, apprehending that they have to fall therein. So ayah 46 describes people who **know** they will be gathered and face their Lord on the Day of Resurrection. And "unto Him they are going to return" means, says Ibn Kathir, that their affairs are all subject to His will and He justly decides what He wills.

**Why this is the hinge.** Ibn Kathir concludes: *since they are certain that they will be returned to Allah and be reckoned, it is easy for them to perform the acts of obedience and refrain from the prohibitions.* The heaviness spoken of in ayah 45, then, is lifted not by a lighter command but by a surer heart.

Ibn Kathir closes with what is recorded in the Sahih: on the Day of Resurrection Allah will say to a servant, "Have I not allowed you to marry, honored you, made the horses and camels subservient to you and allowed you to become a chief and a master?" He will say, "Yes." Allah will say, "Did you have *Zann* (think) that you will meet Me?" He will say, "No." Allah will say, "This Day, I will forget you, just as you forgot Me" — and Ibn Kathir says he will elaborate further on this subject at "They have forgotten Allah, so He has forgotten them" (9:67). Notice how the language of forgetting, which opened this passage in ayah 44, returns here in the mouth of Allah.

## Living it

Preach — but be among the first to implement what you command, as Ibn Jurayj said; and never let your own faults become an excuse for silence. Reach for the two supports Allah named, work on the heart rather than the pose, and keep the meeting with Allah in view: it is for those certain of the return that obedience is made easy.
