# Remember My Favour; Fear a Day of No Intercession

**Sūrah al-Baqarah 2:47–48**

These two ayat are a single movement of thought: first a reminder of an extraordinary privilege, then a warning that the privilege will not save anyone by itself. In ayah 47 Allah tells the Children of Israel to call to mind the favour He placed upon them and the preference He gave them over the nations. In ayah 48 He immediately shuts every door through which a person might hope to escape accountability on the Day of Judgement — no soul availing another, no intercession accepted, no ransom taken, no help given. Ibn Kathir reads the two together exactly this way: after Allah reminded them of the favours He had granted them, He warned them about the torment of the Day of Resurrection. Gift, then reckoning. That is what holds the passage together.

## Ayah 47: "Remember"

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains what "remember" is asking for. It is not nostalgia. Verse 47 asks the Israelites to call to their minds the blessing of Allah **so that the recognition of the benefits they have received may induce them to be thankful to Allah, and thus to obey Him**. Memory is being used as a lever: notice what you were given, and let that noticing turn into gratitude, and let gratitude turn into obedience. Remembering that stops short of changed behaviour has not done its work.

**Addressed to the living, about the dead.** There is a subtlety here that Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out. The verse is addressed to the Jews contemporaneous with the Prophet ﷺ, while the blessing itself had been received by their forefathers. How can they be told to remember a favour they did not personally receive? Because, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, when a man receives a special favour, his children and grandchildren too usually partake of the benefits flowing from it; in that sense the people being addressed may be said to have received the blessing themselves. They were living off an inheritance — and an inheritance is still a gift, still owed thanks.

## What exactly was the favour?

Ibn Kathir specifies it: Allah reminds the Children of Israel of the favours He granted their fathers and grandfathers — **how He showed preference to them by sending them Messengers from among them and revealing Books to them**, more so than to any of the other previous nations. He supports this from elsewhere in the Qur'an, quoting Allah's words *"And We chose them over the ʿĀlamīn (nations) with knowledge"* (44:32), and the speech of Mūsā to his people: *"O my people! Remember the favour of Allah to you: when He made Prophets among you, made you kings, and honoured you above the nations"* (5:20).

From the early generations, Ibn Kathir transmits — through Abū Jaʿfar ar-Rāzī, from ar-Rabīʿ ibn Anas — that **Abū al-ʿĀliyah** explained "and that I preferred you over the ʿĀlamīn" as meaning: *the kingship, Messengers and Books that were granted to them, instead of granting such to the other kingdoms that existed during their time, for every period there is a nation.* Ibn Kathir notes that Mujāhid, ar-Rabīʿ ibn Anas, Qatādah and Ismāʿīl ibn Abī Khālid were reported to have said something similar.

So the favour, as the early commentators named it, had three parts: kingship, Messengers, and Books. And notice the clause Abū al-ʿĀliyah attaches to it — *for every period there is a nation*. The preference is dated from the very moment it is described.

## "Preferred over the worlds" — how far does it reach?

Both of our commentaries are careful here, because the phrase could be misread as an unqualified, permanent superiority.

**Ibn Kathir's approach** is temporal and comparative. He says this is the only way the ayah can be understood, *because this Ummah is better than theirs*, citing Allah's words: *"You are the best of people ever raised up for mankind; you enjoin good and forbid evil, and you believe in Allah. And had the People of the Book believed, it would have been better for them"* (3:110). He also records that the Musnad and Sunan Collections of Hadith reported from Muʿāwiyah ibn Ḥaydah al-Qushayrī that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that the Muslims are the seventieth nation, but are the best and most honoured of them according to Allah. Ibn Kathir adds that there are many hadith on this subject, which he defers to his commentary on 3:110.

**Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's approach** is to limit the scope of the phrase itself: they were given preference *only in certain matters*, or *only over a large part of men* — for example, over the contemporaries of the earlier Israelites.

The two readings converge. The preference was real, but it was bounded — bounded by time and bounded by subject matter. It was never a title deed to permanent favour. And that is precisely what makes the next ayah land so hard.

## Ayah 48: the turn

*"And fear a Day when a person shall not avail another, nor will intercession be accepted from him, nor will compensation be taken from him, nor will they be helped."*

Ibn Kathir identifies "a Day" as the Day of Resurrection. The command is to have *taqwā* of it — to keep your duty to Allah and avoid evil, living now with that Day in view. And then come four negations, one after another, each closing off a different escape route. Read them as a list of everything human beings normally rely on when they are in trouble, being crossed out one by one.

### 1. No soul will avail another

Ibn Kathir: *on that Day, no person shall be of any help to another.* He gathers the parallel verses — *"And no bearer of burdens shall bear another's burden"* (35:18); *"Every man that Day will have enough to make him careless of others"* (80:37); and the address to all humanity: *"O mankind! Have taqwā of your Lord, and fear a Day when no father can avail aught for his son, nor a son avail aught for his father"* (31:33). Ibn Kathir comments that this indeed should serve as a great warning: **both the father and the son will not be of help to each other on that Day.** The closest bond in creation, and it carries no weight there.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the meaning of "avail" concrete and, in doing so, kills a very natural fantasy. The phrase should be understood in the sense of **one man paying the dues on behalf of another man**. Suppose a man is found wanting in the performance of obligatory acts of worship such as Ṣalāh and Ṣawm (fasting), and someone else suggests that his own prayers and fasts be transferred to that man's account to make up the deficiency. *Such a transaction shall not be possible on that day.* Worship is not a transferable currency. Nobody can pray your prayers for you after the ledger closes.

### 2. No intercession will be accepted

This is the phrase that has generated the most discussion, and both sources address it directly.

**Ibn Kathir** reads it in context: *"nor will intercession be accepted from him"* — meaning, **from the disbelievers**. He cites *"So no intercession of intercessors will be of any use to them"* (74:48), and his description of the people of the Fire: *"Now we have no intercessors, nor a close friend"* (26:100–101).

**Maʿārif ul Qurʼān** states the principle plainly: the phrase does not totally deny the possibility of intercession on the Day of Judgement. It only means that **if a man does not have īmān (faith), no intercession in his favour shall be accepted.** The Qur'an itself makes clear in certain other verses that Allah will allow intercession to be made on behalf of some people (it cites 53:26, 34:23 and others), and will disallow it in the case of those who do not possess īmān (21:28, 20:109). And it adds a precise logical point: since there would be no intercession on behalf of the latter at all, the question of its being accepted does not simply arise.

**A doctrinal note.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records that on the basis of this ayah, the Muʿtazilah — and some other groups of a more recent origin — denied the possibility of all intercession in favour of Muslims. Its reply, citing *Bayān al-Qurʼān*, is that the negation of intercession applies only to disbelievers and infidels.

So the ayah is not a locked door for everyone. It is a locked door for the one who arrives without faith.

### 3. No ransom will be taken

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān defines the term simply: ransom means the money paid for securing the release of a criminal — and *this too shall be out of the question*.

Ibn Kathir explains the phrase to mean that Allah does not accept the disbelievers ransoming themselves, and piles up the evidence: *"Verily, those who disbelieved and died while they were disbelievers — the whole earth full of gold will not be accepted from anyone of them, even if they offered it as a ransom"* (3:91); *"if they had all that is in the earth, and as much again with it, to ransom themselves from the torment of the Day of Resurrection, it would never be accepted of them, and theirs would be a painful torment"* (5:36); *"And even if he offers every ransom, it will not be accepted from him"* (6:70); *"So this Day no ransom shall be taken from you, nor from those who disbelieved. Your abode is the Fire"* (57:15).

Ibn Kathir then states the underlying rule: if people do not believe in His Messenger ﷺ and follow what he was sent with, then when they meet Allah on the Day of Resurrection after remaining on the path of disbelief, **their family lineage and the intercession of their masters will not help them at all** — nor would it be accepted of them even if they paid the earth's fill of gold as ransom. He supports this with *"Before a Day comes when there will be no bargaining, nor friendship, nor intercession"* (2:254) and *"On which there will be neither mutual bargaining nor befriending"* (14:31).

Lineage and gold: two things that carry weight in this world. Ibn Kathir names both and rules both out.

### 4. Nor will they be helped

Ibn Kathir explains: no person shall get angry — or anxious — on their behalf and offer them any help, or try to save them from Allah's punishment. As he had stated earlier, neither the relative nor persons of authority will feel pity for the disbelievers, nor will any ransom be accepted for them; consequently they will receive no help from others and will be helpless themselves.

He cites *"While He (Allah) grants refuge, but none grants refuge from Him"* (23:88); *"So on that Day none will punish as He will punish, and none will bind as He will bind"* (89:25–26); the summons *"What is the matter with you? Why do you not help one another?" — "Nay, but that Day they shall surrender"* (37:25–26); and the exposure of false objects of worship: *"Then why did those whom they had taken as gods besides Allah, as a way of approach, not help them? Nay, but they vanished completely from them"* (46:28).

Ibn Kathir also transmits that aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk said that Ibn ʿAbbās said the verse *"What is the matter with you? Why do you not help one another?"* (37:25) means: *"This Day, you shall not have a refuge from Us. Not this Day."*

**Ibn Jarir's summary**, as Ibn Kathir relays it, gathers the whole phrase in one breath: on that Day they shall neither be helped by any helper, nor shall anyone intercede on their behalf; no repeal or ransom will be accepted for them; all courtesy towards them will have ceased, along with any helpful intercession; no type of help or cooperation will be available for them. **The judgement will, on that Day, be up to the Most Great, the Most Just, against whom no intercessor or helper can ever assist. He will then award the evil deed its kind and will multiply the good deeds.**

That last clause deserves a pause. Even in the passage's most severe sentence, the balance is not symmetrical. Evil is repaid in kind; good is multiplied. The Day is terrifying in its justice, but the justice itself is tilted towards generosity.

## Living it

**Privilege is not immunity.** The Children of Israel were told in one breath that they had been given Messengers, Books and kingship — and in the next that on the Day of Judgement nobody avails anybody. The favour did not exempt them from the reckoning; it raised the stakes of it. Any community that inherits religion should read this passage as addressed to itself — and Ibn Kathir does apply the comparison to the Muslim Ummah, which he says is better than theirs. Being part of a favoured community is a reason for gratitude and obedience, never a substitute for it.

**Nothing is transferable.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's illustration is the most practical thing in the passage: no one can move their Ṣalāh or their fasting into your account to make up your deficit. Whatever you intend to bring on that Day, you have to build now, yourself.

**Gratitude is the intended outcome.** Ayah 47 is not asking for a feeling. It is asking that recognition of blessing become thankfulness, and that thankfulness become obedience. If you cannot name what Allah has given you, you will not thank Him for it; if you thank Him only in words, the ayah's purpose is unfinished.

**Faith is the one thing that carries over.** Ibn Kathir's discussion of ayah 48 rules out family lineage, the intercession of masters, and the earth's fill of gold. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the everyday case: "receiving support" usually means getting oneself released from a difficult situation with the help of a strong and powerful friend or patron — and it closes by saying that none of the ways of receiving help possible in this world will be effective in the other world unless one possesses īmān. Every rescue this passage rules out is ruled out for the one who arrives without faith. Which means the whole terrifying list is, read from the other side, an argument for holding onto the one thing that is not on it.
